They are usually the company's newest systems
q.w: They often miss normal patching and monitoring. Inherited legacy systems often sit outside your inventory. Not the public cloud: this was a local system. Not the newest: legacy systems are old ones.

decks.entry: Not disclosed. A legacy system inherited through an acquisition was accessed.
decks.impact: A ransomware gang claims about 100 GB of data. Maersk says the incident is isolated.
decks.lesson: When you buy a company, you inherit its forgotten systems. Find them, then patch, isolate or retire them.

decks.title: Fake job app malware
cards: Key terms

Malware: any malicious software, such as viruses, worms, trojans and spyware.
Sideloading: installing an app from outside the official app store, such as from a link.
Accessibility access: an Android permission meant for assistive tools, which can let an app read and control your screen.
Factory reset: wiping a phone back to its original settings, deleting all apps and data.
What happened

On 4 November 2026, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) New Zealand issued a warning. Malicious actors are spreading Android malware disguised as a job-seeking app. It can also be disguised as a banking app.
How they got in
Fake jobs are advertised on social media. The chat then moves to a messaging app, with a link to download another app. Victims sideload it, meaning they install it from outside the Play Store.
How the app takes over
The app shows a fake Google Play update page. Then it asks for permissions, especially Accessibility access. That permission can let it read and control your screen.
Impact
NCSC hasn't named the app. It also hasn't said how many New Zealanders were affected.
Removing the malware
Uninstalling the app may not fully remove the malware, NCSC warns, because it can install more. A factory reset, which wipes the phone, is more likely to work.
Lesson: no unknown sources
Never enable installs from unknown sources. Install apps from the Play Store only.
Lesson: jobs don't need apps
A real employer won't need you to install an app from a link. Be wary of any job offer that moves to private chat.
Lesson: question Accessibility
Be very wary of any app asking for Accessibility access. That permission can let it read and control your screen.
decks.maps: CSF PR.AT awareness and training · CSF PR.PS device settings

q.q: A recruiter on social media asks you to install their "jobs app" from a link. What's the safest move?
o: Decline, and check the company's official site
Install it, but deny any permission it asks for
Install it, then uninstall it if anything looks odd
q.w: Decline and check the company's official site, so the malware never reaches your phone. Not installing and denying permissions: the malware is already on your phone. Not uninstalling later: NCSC warns that may not remove it.

decks.entry: A fake job app sideloaded from a link sent in a messaging app.
decks.impact: Malware with Accessibility access that can install more malware.
decks.lesson: Only install apps from the Play Store, and be wary of jobs that move to private chat.

decks.title: SSH quick check
cards: Check your SSH login setting

Run `sudo sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication` to see the setting sshd, the Secure Shell (SSH) server, is actually using. The result `passwordauthentication no` blocks SSHole-style password bypasses. Check any Match blocks too. They can turn passwords back on for some users.

decks.title: AWS trust policies
cards: Spot the mistake: a trust policy

An Identity and Access Management (IAM) role trusts `arn:aws:iam::111122223333:root`, a vendor's account, with no conditions. The mistake: here, `:root` means the vendor's whole account, not its root user. Name the vendor's exact role instead. If the vendor publishes fixed IP addresses, allow only those. Delete the role once you stop using the vendor.

decks.title: CloudTrail logging
cards: S3 reads go unlogged by default

AWS CloudTrail records management events by default. But S3 object reads are "data events", which you must turn on. When attackers abused Qubole's AWS access, some victims couldn't tell which files were taken.

decks.title: NCSC NZ threat report
cards: NZ by the numbers (2025/26)

In 2025/26, New Zealand's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC NZ) flagged 369 incidents of potential national significance, up from 331. It also recorded 4 "highly significant" incidents. That's as many as in the previous ten years combined.

decks.title: CISA KEV
cards: KEV means "it's being used now"

The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue, run by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), lists flaws with evidence of real-world exploitation. US federal civilian agencies get fixed deadlines. SSHole, an OpenSSH flaw, was due 12 November 2026, 3 days after listing. Everyone else should treat KEV as a "patch first" list.

decks.title: where and project
cards: Reading a query
Kusto Query Language (KQL) runs in Microsoft Sentinel, Defender and Log Analytics. A KQL query starts with a table. Each `|`, called a pipe, passes the rows on to the next step, top to bottom.

SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4625
| project TimeGenerated, Account, IpAddress, Computer
Filter, then choose columns

In a KQL query, `where` keeps only the rows that match. `project` picks the columns you want to see. Filter as early as you can, because smaller tables are faster and cheaper. You can practise free in Microsoft's Log Analytics demo (aka.ms/LADemo).

q.q: In this query, which line keeps only failed logons?
q.code:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4625
| project TimeGenerated, Account, IpAddress, Computer
o: `SecurityEvent`
`| where EventID == 4625`
`| project TimeGenerated, Account, IpAddress, Computer`
q.w: The `where` line. `where` filters rows, and Event ID 4625 is a failed logon. Not `project`: it only chooses columns. Not `SecurityEvent`: that's the table the query starts from.

decks.title: Counting with summarize
cards: Group and count
In Kusto Query Language (KQL), `summarize count() by X` groups rows by X and counts each group. Use it to find the busiest senders, the most-targeted accounts and noisy sources.

SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4625
| summarize count() by IpAddress
| top 10 by count_
The count_ column

`count()` makes a column named `count_`. To see the biggest first, use `top 10 by count_` or `sort by count_ desc`. In Splunk, the rough equivalent is `index=wineventlog EventCode=4625 | stats count by src`.

q.q: You want failed logons per source IP, biggest first. Which line goes after `where EventID == 4625`?
o: `| project IpAddress | sort by IpAddress desc`
`| summarize count() by IpAddress | sort by count_ desc`
`| take 100 | summarize count() by IpAddress | sort by count_ desc`
q.w: The `summarize` line. It groups and counts, and sorting by `count_` puts the noisiest first. Not `project`: it lists addresses without counting them. Not `take 100` first: it counts only 100 arbitrary rows.

decks.title: Time windows: ago and bin
cards: Search recent data only
In Kusto Query Language (KQL), `ago(1h)` means one hour before now. Put `where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)` near the top of a query to search only recent data.

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventID == 4625
| summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
Buckets of time
`bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)` rounds each timestamp down into 5-minute buckets. That makes a burst of events stand out. Add `| render timechart` in Log Analytics to see it as a chart.

q.q: What does `bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)` do?
o: Waits 5 minutes before running
Groups events into 5-minute buckets
Deletes events older than 5 minutes
q.w: Groups events into 5-minute buckets. Bucketing by time turns a list of events into a pattern you can spot, like a spike of failures. Not deleting: `bin` only groups, and nothing is deleted. Not waiting: `bin` doesn't delay the query.

decks.title: has versus contains
cards: Whole terms

In Kusto Query Language (KQL), `has` matches a whole term. It's fast because Log Analytics indexes terms. `ProcessCommandLine has "-enc"` finds the switch as a separate term. Attackers vary the switch (`-e`, `-EncodedCommand`), so real hunts check several.

DeviceProcessEvents
| where FileName =~ "powershell.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-enc"
Any substring
`contains` matches any part of the text, so it's slower. Both `has` and `contains` are case-insensitive. `has_cs` and `contains_cs` are the case-sensitive versions. `=~` is a case-insensitive equals.

q.q: Does `"powershell.exe -nop" has "power"` return true?
o: Yes, but only in upper case
Yes, because has matches any substring
No, because power isn't a whole term there
q.w: No, because power isn't a whole term there. `has` looks for whole terms. `contains "power"` would match, because it checks substrings. The substring answer is the trap: it describes `contains`, not `has`. Case doesn't matter, because `has` is case-insensitive.

decks.title: Sign-ins in SigninLogs
cards: Where sign-ins are logged

Microsoft Entra sign-ins land in `SigninLogs`. App background sign-ins go to AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs. ResultType "0" is success. Any other code is a failure or interruption, like 50126 (bad username or password).

SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "50126"
| summarize users = dcount(UserPrincipalName), failures = count() by IPAddress
| where users > 10
Spray or targeted attack?

To spot the attack type, count distinct users failing from each IP. Many users failing from one IP is password spraying: one common password tried on many accounts. Many failures on one user from many IPs is a targeted attack.

q.q: In SigninLogs, what does ResultType "0" mean?
o: A failed password
A blocked country
A successful sign-in
q.w: A successful sign-in. Zero means no error. Anything else is a failure or interruption, and the code tells you why. Not a failed password: that has its own code, such as 50126. Not a blocked country: that's a failure, so its code isn't zero.

decks.title: Process creation (4688)
cards: The event
Windows Event ID 4688 records a new process. With command-line auditing turned on, it also includes the full command line. That's where attackers' encoded PowerShell shows up.

SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "-enc"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
Turn it on first

Event 4688 needs the “Audit Process Creation” policy turned on. Command lines also need the Group Policy setting “Include command line in process creation events”. Defender for Endpoint records them in DeviceProcessEvents without that step.

q.q: Your 4688 events have an empty CommandLine column. What's the likely cause?
o: The process never actually ran
Command-line auditing isn't turned on
Kusto Query Language (KQL) can't read command lines
q.w: Command-line auditing isn't turned on. Event 4688 records the process, but the command line only appears once the audit policy setting is enabled. Not a process that never ran: 4688 only records processes that started. Not KQL: it reads whatever the event contains.

decks.title: Role changes in AuditLogs
cards: Where Entra changes are logged

Microsoft Entra ID changes, such as new users and role assignments, land in `AuditLogs`. Alert when someone joins a powerful role. Matching “member to role” also catches Privileged Identity Management (PIM) activations.

AuditLogs
| where OperationName has "member to role"
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, Actor, TargetResources
Reading nested data

Some columns, like InitiatedBy, hold nested data in JavaScript Object Notation (JSON). In Kusto Query Language (KQL), reach into them with dots. Then wrap the value in `tostring()` so you can filter or project it.

q.q: Why alert when someone is added to Global Administrator?
o: It happens thousands of times a day
Global Administrator has no real power
It's a common way attackers keep control
q.w: It's a common way attackers keep control of a tenant, an organisation's Entra ID. New admin role members are rare and powerful, so alerting on them is high-value and low-noise. Not the others: these changes are rare, and Global Administrator is highly privileged.

decks.title: Joining two results
cards: Failures then a success
In Kusto Query Language (KQL), `join` combines two result sets on a shared column. This example finds sources with many failed logons that also had a successful logon.

let fails = SecurityEvent
  | where EventID == 4625
  | summarize failures = count() by IpAddress
  | where failures > 20;
fails
| join kind=inner (
    SecurityEvent | where EventID == 4624 | distinct IpAddress
  ) on IpAddress
let and inner joins

`let` names a result so you can reuse it. `kind=inner` keeps only rows found in both sides. So you see just the sources that failed a lot and also logged on successfully at some point. It doesn't check which came first.

q.q: A query joins a list of IPs with many failed logons to a list of IPs with a successful logon, using `join kind=inner ... on IpAddress`. What does it return?
o: IPs found in both lists
Every IP from both tables
Only IPs that never succeeded
q.w: IPs found in both lists. An inner join keeps matches from both sides: many failures and at least one success, the shape of a guessed password. Not every IP: an inner join drops rows without a match. Not IPs that never succeeded: those have no match.

decks.title: Equifax
decks.entry: An unpatched Apache Struts flaw (CVE-2017-5638) in an online dispute portal.
decks.impact: Personal data on about 147 million people was stolen.
decks.lesson: Patch known, critical flaws on internet-facing apps within days, not months.
cards: Key terms

Patch: an update that fixes a flaw in software.
Apache Struts: free, open-source code for building web apps.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE): an ID that names one publicly known vulnerability.
Certificate: a file that binds a domain name to a public key, signed by a certificate authority.
What happened
Between May and July 2017, attackers stole personal data from credit agency Equifax. It included names, birth dates and US Social Security numbers. About 147 million people were affected.
How they got in

Attackers exploited a flaw in Apache Struts on a public dispute portal. The flaw's Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) ID is CVE-2017-5638. A fix had been published in March 2017, but that system hadn't been patched.
Why it went unnoticed

An expired certificate stopped a device from checking encrypted traffic. That device's job was to inspect the traffic. The certificate had been expired for about 19 months. Once it was renewed, staff saw suspicious traffic within a day.
Lesson: know where it runs
Know where every component runs, so you can patch fast. The Struts fix was out for about two months before the attack began, but the dispute portal wasn't patched.
Lesson: watch certificate expiry
Monitor certificate expiry on your security tools. A silent failure looks the same as no attack.
decks.maps: A03 Software Supply Chain Failures · A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures

q.q: What let attackers into Equifax?
o: An unpatched Apache Struts flaw
A laptop stolen from a staff member
A phishing email to the chief executive
q.w: An unpatched Apache Struts flaw. The fix had been out for about two months, but the dispute portal wasn't patched. Not a stolen laptop or phishing: attackers came in through the public dispute portal.

decks.title: SolarWinds
decks.entry: Malicious code slipped into the SolarWinds Orion build and shipped in signed updates.
decks.impact: Fewer than 18,000 customers may have installed the backdoor. Far fewer were targeted further.
decks.lesson: Protect the build pipeline as carefully as production, and watch what trusted software does.
decks.source: SolarWinds SEC filing and CISA, 2020 to 2021
cards: Key terms

Software supply chain: everything that goes into your software, such as libraries, build tools, pipelines and the people who maintain them.
Build system: the servers and tools that turn source code into the software customers install.
Backdoor: hidden code that gives an attacker secret access.
Code signing: signing software so users can check who made it and that it wasn't changed.
What happened
In December 2020, security firm FireEye found it had been breached. The trail led to SolarWinds Orion. Orion is an IT monitoring product used by governments and large companies.
How they got in

Attackers got into SolarWinds' build system, which turns source code into the software customers install. They inserted a backdoor, later called SUNBURST, into Orion updates. The updates were signed, so they looked legitimate.
Impact

SolarWinds told the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) that fewer than 18,000 customers may have installed the affected updates. The attackers then picked a much smaller set of targets for deeper access. These included US government agencies.
Timing and attribution
Attackers were in SolarWinds' network from late 2019. The US government blamed Russia's foreign intelligence service (SVR).
Lesson: signed isn't always safe
A signed update can still be malicious if the build itself is compromised. A signature proves who built the software, not that the build was clean.
Lesson: lock down build systems
Protect build systems as carefully as production systems. At SolarWinds, the build is where the backdoor got in.
Lesson: watch trusted software
Check what the software you trust is doing. Limit what monitoring tools, such as Orion, can reach.
decks.maps: A03 Software Supply Chain Failures · A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures

q.q: Why did customers trust the SolarWinds backdoor?
o: It came in a signed Orion update
Customers had turned off antivirus
It came in an email from SolarWinds
q.w: It came in a signed Orion update. The backdoor was added during the build, so the update carried SolarWinds' real signature. Not an email: it arrived as a normal update. Not disabled antivirus: customers trusted it because it was signed.

decks.title: Colonial Pipeline
decks.entry: A password for an old VPN account that didn't require MFA.
decks.impact: The largest fuel pipeline on the US East Coast shut down for about five days.
decks.lesson: Remove unused accounts and require MFA on every remote access path.
decks.source: US Senate testimony and US DOJ, 2021
cards: Key terms

Ransomware: malware that locks or steals data and demands payment.
Double extortion: ransomware that steals data and then encrypts it, so attackers can threaten to leak it as well as lock it.
Virtual private network (VPN): a secure link that lets staff log in to a work network remotely.
Operational technology (OT): systems that control physical equipment, such as pipelines and factory machines.
What happened
In May 2021, the DarkSide ransomware group hit Colonial Pipeline. The company shut down its fuel pipeline as a precaution. That caused fuel shortages and panic buying in the US South East.
How they got in

Colonial's chief executive told the US Senate that the attackers used the password for a legacy virtual private network (VPN) account. The account was no longer in use but still active. It didn't have multi-factor authentication (MFA).
Impact
The pipeline was shut for about five days. Colonial paid a ransom of 75 bitcoin, about US$4.4 million at the time. The US Justice Department later recovered about 63.7 bitcoin of it.
Double extortion
DarkSide also stole about 100 GB of data before encrypting. That made this double extortion: the attackers could threaten to leak the data as well as lock it.
Lesson: clean up old accounts
Remove accounts nobody uses. Colonial's legacy VPN account was no longer in use, but it still worked.
Lesson: MFA on remote access
Require MFA on every remote access path. At Colonial, a password alone was enough to get in.
Lesson: separate IT and OT
Ransomware hit IT systems, but the business shut down operations because it couldn't be sure they were safe. Separate IT from operational technology (OT), the systems that run physical equipment.
decks.maps: A07 Authentication Failures · CSF PR.AA identity management

q.q: What weakness let DarkSide into Colonial Pipeline?
o: An unpatched pipeline controller
An unused VPN account with no MFA
A malicious USB stick in the office
q.w: An unused VPN account with no MFA. It was still active and only needed a password. Not a pipeline controller: ransomware hit IT systems, not the pipeline itself. Not a USB stick: the attackers logged in remotely.

decks.title: Optus
decks.entry: An internet-facing API that returned customer data without asking for any authentication.
decks.impact: Personal data on about 9.5 million current and former customers was taken.
decks.lesson: Every API needs authentication and access control, including old or forgotten ones.
cards: Key terms

Application programming interface (API): a way for programs to ask another system for data over a network.
Authentication: checking proof that you are who you claim to be.
Broken access control: an app failing to check what a logged-in user is allowed to see or do.
Subdomain: a name under a main domain, such as api.example.com under example.com.
What happened

In September 2022, Australian telco Optus disclosed that customer data had been accessed. It included names, birth dates and phone numbers. For many customers, it also included passport or driver licence numbers.
How they got in
The data came from an application programming interface (API) that didn't require authentication. The API was reachable from the internet.
What the regulator alleged
The Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) took Optus to court. It alleged that a 2018 coding error left the API's access control broken for years.
Impact
About 9.5 million current and former customers were affected. Many had to replace ID documents. ACMA and the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) both took Optus to court.
Lesson: inventory every API
Optus reportedly fixed the same error on its main domain in 2021, but missed a dormant subdomain. Keep an inventory of every API and domain.
Lesson: test access control
Test access control on every API, including old or forgotten ones. An API with no authentication lets anyone request customer records.
Lesson: delete ID numbers
Delete ID numbers once you no longer need them. Data you no longer hold can't be stolen.
decks.maps: A01 Broken Access Control

q.q: What was wrong with the Optus API?
o: It ran on an unpatched server
It didn't require authentication
It used weak, outdated encryption
q.w: It didn't require authentication. Anyone who found it could request customer records. Not encryption: access control was missing, not broken encryption. Not an unpatched server: the problem was missing access control, not old software.

decks.title: MGM Resorts
decks.entry: A phone call to the IT help desk, pretending to be an employee, to get their login and MFA reset.
decks.impact: Hotel and casino systems were disrupted for days. MGM expected a hit to earnings of about US$100 million.
decks.lesson: Help desks need strong identity checks before resetting passwords or MFA.
cards: Key terms

Social engineering: tricking people into doing something that helps an attacker, such as approving a login.
Vishing: phishing by phone call.
Multi-factor authentication (MFA): proving who you are with two or more different kinds of proof, such as a password and a phone.
Ransomware: malware that locks or steals data and demands payment.
What happened
In September 2023, a cyberattack disrupted MGM Resorts' hotels and casinos in Las Vegas. Digital room keys, slot machines and booking systems stopped working for days.
How they got in

The attackers called MGM's IT help desk, posing as an employee. They got the help desk to reset that employee's login and multi-factor authentication (MFA). This is vishing, meaning phishing by phone call.
Who was behind it
The attackers were linked to the group known as Scattered Spider. The ALPHV/BlackCat ransomware group claimed involvement.
Impact

MGM said it expected a hit to earnings of about US$100 million. It said some customer personal data was taken. Reports say it refused to pay a ransom. Caesars Entertainment was hit by the same group weeks earlier and reportedly paid.
Lesson: attackers call in
Attackers don't always break in. Sometimes they call in.
Lesson: verify before resets
Verify identity properly before any password or MFA reset. For example, call back on a known number or get a manager's approval.
decks.maps: A07 Authentication Failures · CSF PR.AT awareness and training

q.q: How did the MGM attackers first get access?
o: They hacked a slot machine
They phoned the IT help desk
They guessed an admin password
q.w: They phoned the IT help desk. Posing as an employee, they got that person's login and MFA reset. Not a slot machine: those stopped working after the attack began. Not a guessed password: the help desk reset it for them.

decks.title: Snowflake customer breaches
decks.entry: Passwords stolen by infostealers, used on accounts with no MFA.
decks.impact: Snowflake and Mandiant notified about 165 organisations, including AT&T, Ticketmaster and Santander.
decks.lesson: Under shared responsibility, securing your own cloud accounts is your job. Turn on MFA and network rules.
cards: Key terms

Infostealer: malware that steals saved passwords and login data from a computer.
Credentials: the details you log in with, such as a username and password.
Multi-factor authentication (MFA): proving who you are with two or more different kinds of proof, such as a password and a phone.
Shared responsibility model: the split of security duties between a cloud provider and its customers.
What happened
In mid-2024, attackers stole large amounts of data from customers of Snowflake, a cloud data platform. Victims included AT&T, Ticketmaster and Santander.
How they got in

Mandiant found the attackers logged in to customer accounts with credentials stolen by infostealer malware. Some credentials dated back to 2020. The accounts didn't have multi-factor authentication (MFA), and many had no network restrictions.
Impact
Snowflake and Mandiant notified about 165 organisations. Snowflake and its investigators found no evidence that Snowflake's own platform was breached.
Lesson: accounts are your job
Under the shared responsibility model, protecting accounts is the customer's job. The model splits security duties between the cloud provider and its customers.
Lesson: MFA, rotation, networks
Require MFA, rotate old credentials and limit logins to known networks. Some credentials used against Snowflake customers dated back to 2020.
Lesson: secure by default
Snowflake later made MFA the default for new accounts. Secure defaults protect customers who never change their settings.
decks.maps: A07 Authentication Failures · cloud shared responsibility

q.q: How did attackers get into Snowflake customers' data?
o: A malicious Snowflake software update
Stolen passwords on accounts with no MFA
A zero-day flaw in the Snowflake platform
q.w: Stolen passwords on accounts with no MFA. Infostealers had taken the passwords, some as far back as 2020. Not an update or a zero-day, a flaw attackers use before a fix exists: no evidence showed Snowflake's own platform was breached.

decks.title: WannaCry
decks.entry: A worm using EternalBlue on unpatched SMBv1, fixed by MS17-010.
decks.impact: More than 200,000 computers in about 150 countries, including about a third of NHS trusts in England.
decks.lesson: Patch fast, turn off SMBv1 and never expose SMB to the internet.
decks.source: UK National Audit Office and US DOJ, 2017 to 2018
cards: Key terms

Ransomware: malware that locks or steals data and demands payment.
Worm: malware that spreads between computers on its own, with no clicks needed.
Server Message Block (SMB): the Windows file-sharing protocol.
Kill switch: a built-in check that makes malware stop, such as when a certain domain responds.
What happened
On 12 May 2017, WannaCry ransomware spread around the world in hours. It encrypted files and demanded bitcoin. Hospitals, factories and telcos were hit.
How it spread

WannaCry was a worm, so it jumped between computers with no clicks needed. It used EternalBlue to attack Windows Server Message Block version 1 (SMBv1). EternalBlue was a US National Security Agency (NSA) exploit, leaked by the Shadow Brokers in April 2017.
A fix already existed
Microsoft had released the fix, MS17-010, in March 2017. That was about two months before WannaCry spread.
Impact
More than 200,000 computers in about 150 countries were hit. In England, at least 81 of 236 National Health Service (NHS) trusts were affected. About 19,000 appointments were cancelled.
Who was blamed
The US and UK governments later attributed WannaCry to North Korea.
How it was slowed
Researcher Marcus Hutchins slowed WannaCry by registering a domain that acted as a kill switch.
Lesson: patch fast
Patch fast. Unpatched computers were still open to WannaCry about two months after the fix came out.
Lesson: segment the network
Unpatched systems on a flat network let one infection reach everything. Segment the network, meaning split it into zones with rules that limit traffic between them.
Lesson: switch off SMBv1
Turn off SMBv1, and never expose SMB to the internet. WannaCry attacked SMBv1 to jump between computers.
decks.maps: Essential Eight: patch operating systems · A02 Security Misconfiguration (SMBv1 left on)

q.q: How did WannaCry spread so fast?
o: Through infected USB sticks
Through a worm attacking SMBv1
Through a flood of phishing emails
q.w: Through a worm attacking SMBv1. EternalBlue let it jump between unpatched computers on its own, with no user action. Not USB sticks or phishing: both need a person to act, and WannaCry didn't.

decks.title: Windows Event IDs
cards: Logons
Event ID 4624 is a successful logon and 4625 is a failed one. Both are in the Security log. Logon type 2 is at the keyboard, 3 is over the network (like a file share) and 10 is Remote Desktop.
Privilege and accounts

Event ID 4672 means special privileges were assigned to a new logon, which usually means an admin logged on. 4720 is a new user account. 4732 is a member added to a local security group, such as Administrators. 4740 is an account locked out.
Red flags

Event ID 1102 means the Security audit log was cleared. 7045, in the System log, means a new service was installed. 4688 is a new process. 4104 is PowerShell script block logging, which shows the script that actually ran.

qs.q: Which Event ID records a failed Windows logon?
qs.w: 4625. It records a failed logon in the Security log. Not 4624: that's a successful logon. Not 4672: that's special privileges assigned to a new logon, usually an admin.

qs.q: What does a 4624 event with logon type 10 mean?
o: A Remote Desktop logon
A logon at the keyboard
A logon to a file share
qs.w: A Remote Desktop logon. Type 10 is RemoteInteractive, which is Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). Not the keyboard or a file share: type 2 is interactive and type 3 is network.

qs.q: Why is Event ID 1102 a red flag?
o: An account was locked out
The Security log was cleared
A new user account was created
qs.w: The Security audit log was cleared. Clearing the log is a common way to hide tracks, so treat it as suspicious unless it was planned. Not a lockout or a new user: those are 4740 and 4720.

decks.title: A new local admin
cards: The evidence

These are a file server's Security log events at 2:14am, simplified. Your security information and event management (SIEM) system collected them before the log was cleared. Nobody on the team was working. Logon type 10 means Remote Desktop. svc_backup is a service account, which software uses to log in instead of a person.

4624  type 10  svc_backup
4720  created user: helpdesk2
4732  helpdesk2 added to
      Administrators
1102  audit log cleared

qs.q: What's the most worrying sign here?
o: A logon at 2:14am with nobody working
A service account logging on remotely
A new admin account, then a cleared log
qs.w: A new admin account, then a cleared log. Creating an admin account is classic persistence, a way to keep access. Clearing the log afterwards is covering tracks. Not the late logon or the service account alone: either can have an innocent reason.

qs.q: What should you check first?
o: Whether the server needs a reboot
Where svc_backup's logon came from
How much disk space the server has
qs.w: Where svc_backup's logon came from. A service account using Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) at night is unusual. Check its source address, its history and whether it should ever use RDP. A reboot or disk space won't reveal a stolen account.

qs.q: Which ATT&CK techniques fit events 4720 and 1102?
o: T1136 Create Account and T1070 Indicator Removal
T1566 Phishing and T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact
T1110 Brute Force and T1046 Network Service Discovery
qs.w: T1136 Create Account and T1070 Indicator Removal. Event 4720 is a new account, a persistence step. Event 1102 is a cleared log, which removes evidence. The others don't fit: nothing shows phishing, encryption, password guessing or scanning.

after: What to do
Disable helpdesk2 and remove it from Administrators. Reset the svc_backup password. Isolate the server if you see more, and escalate. Check other servers for the same account name.

decks.title: Searching in Splunk
cards: Search first, then pipe
Splunk's Search Processing Language (SPL) starts with a search. Then each `|` passes results to the next command, as in Kusto Query Language (KQL). Field names depend on how your data was indexed.

index=wineventlog EventCode=4625
| table _time user src
KQL and SPL side by side

KQL and SPL share one idea: filter first, then choose columns. In KQL: `SecurityEvent | where EventID == 4625 | project TimeGenerated, Account`. In SPL: `index=wineventlog EventCode=4625 | table _time user`.

q.q: In SPL, what does `| table _time user src` do?
o: Counts the rows
Shows only those columns
Deletes the other fields from the index
q.w: Shows only those columns. `table` picks the columns to display, like `project` in KQL. Not counting: that's a job for `stats count`. Not deleting: `table` only changes what you see, and nothing is deleted from the index.

decks.title: Counting with stats
cards: stats count by

In Splunk's Search Processing Language (SPL), `stats count by src` groups events by source and counts each group. It works like `summarize count() by` in Kusto Query Language (KQL). Add `| sort - count` to put the biggest first.

index=wineventlog EventCode=4625
| stats count by src
| sort - count
| head 10
Filter the result
`| where count > 20` keeps only the noisy sources after counting, the same as a `where` after `summarize` in KQL.

q.q: Which SPL finds the ten sources with the most failed logons?
o: `EventCode=4625 | table src count | sort - count | head 10`
`EventCode=4625 | stats count by src | sort - count | head 10`
`EventCode=4625 | head 10 | stats count by src | sort - count`
q.w: The `stats` query. It counts per source, sorts in descending order, then keeps the top ten. Not `table`: it creates no count. Not `head 10` first: it keeps ten events before counting.

decks.title: Time in Splunk
cards: Search recent data only

In Splunk's Search Processing Language (SPL), adding `earliest=-1h` to the search limits it to the last hour. It works like `where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)` in Kusto Query Language (KQL). Searching less time is faster.
index=wineventlog EventCode=4625 earliest=-1h
Buckets of time
`timechart span=5m count` counts events in five-minute buckets. It works like `summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)` in KQL. Spikes stand out on a chart.

q.q: What does `timechart span=5m count` give you?
o: The five most common values
Events from the last five minutes only
A count per five-minute window
q.w: A count per five-minute window. `span` sets the bucket size. Not the last five minutes: `earliest` sets how far back to search. Not the most common values: `timechart` counts events over time.

decks.title: Extracting fields with rex
cards: rex

In Splunk's Search Processing Language (SPL), `rex` pulls out a field that isn't extracted for you. It uses a regular expression, a pattern that matches text, with a named group. Named groups work like the capture groups in Terminal Lesson 12.

index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure "Failed password"
| rex "from (?<src_ip>\S+)"
| stats count by src_ip
Named groups
`(?<src_ip>\S+)` saves whatever matched into a new field called src_ip. You can then count, sort or table it like any other field.

q.q: In `rex "from (?<src_ip>\S+)"`, what is src_ip?
o: The index that the search reads from
A new field holding the text after "from"
A built-in field that Splunk extracts by itself
q.w: A new field holding the text after "from". The named group creates the field from whatever the pattern matches. Not the index: the search names that with `index=linux`. Not a built-in field: `rex` creates src_ip because Splunk didn't extract it.

decks.title: Optimizely script hijack hits Australian sites
cards: Key terms

Third-party script: code from another company that runs on your website.
Card skimmer: hidden code that copies payment card details as people type them.
Content delivery network (CDN): servers that deliver a company's files quickly to visitors.
Content Security Policy (CSP): a website setting that limits where the page may load scripts from.
What happened

On 16 November 2026 (UTC), an attacker added malicious JavaScript to websites using Optimizely Web Experimentation. Optimizely is a tool for testing changes to websites. Researchers at Report URI found the code on sites of 178 organisations. Optimizely confirmed the attack.
How they got in

Optimizely says the attacker exploited a flaw in its Experimentation account signup flow. The code went into the Project JavaScript field, which runs on every page view. It was served from Optimizely's own content delivery network (CDN), which sites already allowed.
Impact

Researchers say the code swapped crypto wallet addresses and copied card numbers, expiry dates and card security codes (CVV). No count of stolen cards has been published. Optimizely says fewer than 5% of its customers were affected.
The Australian sites

Researchers' lists include Vodafone Australia and HSBC Australia. HSBC says the scripts weren't active on its websites. TPG Telecom, which owns Vodafone Australia, paused Optimizely as a precaution. It told iTnews it found no evidence Vodafone systems or customer data were compromised.
Lesson: every script is your code
A script you load from a supplier runs with the same power as your own code. Keep a list of every third-party script on your pages. Remove the ones you no longer use.
Lesson: a strict CSP

Report URI says 24 organisations blocked the payload with a strict Content Security Policy (CSP). It limits which sites a page can load scripts from. Allowing a supplier's whole CDN gives less protection.
Lesson: keep card fields off your page
Use your payment provider's hosted card fields where you can. In this attack, the skimmer couldn't read card fields hosted by a separate provider.
decks.maps: A03 Software Supply Chain Failures · A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures · NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) GV.SC supply chain risk

q.q: A skimmer like this one runs on a shop's checkout page. Which card fields are out of its reach?
o: Fields on pages served over HTTPS
Fields in the shop's own payment form
Fields hosted by a separate payment provider
q.w: Fields hosted by a separate payment provider. The skimmer could only read fields in the site's own forms. Not the shop's own form: that's what it copied. Not HTTPS: it protects data in transit, not from scripts on the page.

decks.entry: A flaw in Optimizely's signup flow let an attacker add code to customer projects.
decks.impact: Malicious code ran on websites of 178 organisations, including Australian brands.
decks.lesson: Treat third-party scripts as your own code. Limit them with a strict CSP.
decks.source: Optimizely status page and Report URI, 2026

decks.title: Microsoft agent-framework package poisoned on PyPI
cards: Key terms

Python Package Index (PyPI): the main public site for sharing Python packages.
Credential stealer: malware that hunts for passwords, keys and tokens, then sends them to an attacker.
.pth file: a small file Python reads every time it starts. It can run code.
Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD): automated systems that build, test and ship code.
What happened

On 17 November 2026 (UTC), two malicious versions of Microsoft's official agent-framework package appeared on the Python Package Index (PyPI). They were versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, published 33 minutes apart. PyPI has quarantined both. Version 1.26.0 is the last clean release.
How they got in

The bad releases came through Microsoft's real project, not a lookalike name. Microsoft hasn't said how the attacker got permission to publish. Researchers say the bad releases were packed outside Microsoft's normal release process.
Why it ran without being used
Each bad release added a .pth file. Python runs import lines in .pth files every time it starts. So the stealer ran even if your code never imported the package.
Impact

The malware hunted for cloud and developer secrets. These included Azure and GitHub credentials, plus continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) secrets. No count of affected users has been published.
Lesson: pin exact versions

Pin exact versions in your requirements file, such as agent-framework==1.26.0. A loose rule like >=1.26.0 would have pulled in a bad release automatically. Pinning with hashes, using a lockfile, is stronger still.
Lesson: removing it isn't enough
Uninstalling the package doesn't make stolen keys safe. Rotate every secret the machine or pipeline could reach. Then rebuild from a clean environment.
decks.maps: A03 Software Supply Chain Failures · NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) GV.SC supply chain risk · CSF PR.AA identity and access

q.q: You installed agent-framework 1.26.1 on a build server yesterday. What's the most important next step?
o: Upgrade to the next release
Uninstall the package and carry on
Rotate the secrets the server held
q.w: Rotate the secrets the server held. The stealer ran at startup, so assume they were taken. Uninstalling stops it running again but doesn't undo the theft. Upgrading is the trap answer: it doesn't undo the theft, and 1.26.2 was also malicious.

decks.entry: Two poisoned releases were published under Microsoft's real PyPI project.
decks.impact: A credential stealer ran on every Python start where they were installed.
decks.lesson: Pin exact versions. Rotate secrets after a bad install.

decks.title: COLD RELIC: one cloud breach used to hit another
cards: Key terms

Super Admin: the top admin role in Google Workspace, with control over every account.
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) fatigue: sending many sign-in prompts until the person approves one to make them stop.
Passkey: a phishing-resistant sign-in key stored on your device, used instead of a password.
Impersonation: pretending to be someone the target already knows and trusts.
What happened

On 17 November 2026, Google described attacks by a Russian state-backed espionage group it calls COLD RELIC. The group broke into one US organisation's Google Workspace. It then used the stolen data to break into a second US organisation. Neither victim has been named.
How they got in

At the first organisation, the group had stolen the password for a Super Admin account. It then sent repeated multi-factor authentication (MFA) push prompts until one was approved. Push approvals are a weak form of MFA, because a tired person can tap yes.
How they stayed in

Once inside, the group added its own passkeys, backup codes and MFA devices to the account. These kept its access working after password and session resets. Passkeys weren't the weakness here. The attacker registered its own after taking over the account.
Impact

Using Super Admin rights, the group exported the staff directory and started a domain-wide Google Workspace export. It then posed as a real staff member of the first organisation to contact the second one on an encrypted messaging app.
Lesson: protect admin accounts first
Give Super Admin accounts phishing-resistant MFA, such as FIDO2 security keys or passkeys. Push prompts can be approved by mistake. Keep the number of Super Admins small.
Lesson: control new MFA devices
Google recommends checks before a new MFA device or passkey is added. Require approval from an existing admin, or confirm the person's identity another way.
Lesson: clean up after a takeover
Resetting the password isn't enough. Revoke sessions and app access (OAuth grants). Remove any passkeys, backup codes or MFA devices you don't recognise.
Lesson: check unexpected contact
A message from a known contact can still come from an attacker using stolen data. Check unusual requests through a separate channel you already trust.
decks.maps: A07 Authentication Failures · NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) PR.AA identity and access · CSF DE.CM continuous monitoring

q.q: After the takeover, the victim resets the Super Admin password. Why might the attacker still get in?
o: The reset doesn't apply to admin roles
The attacker's own passkey is still enrolled
Google Workspace keeps the old password active
q.w: The attacker's own passkey is still enrolled. Passkeys and backup codes work without the password, so remove unknown ones too. Not the admin role or the old password: the reset worked, but the attacker had another way in.

decks.entry: Stolen Super Admin credentials, then repeated MFA push prompts until one was approved.
decks.impact: Staff directory and Workspace data exported, then used to target a second organisation.
decks.lesson: Use phishing-resistant MFA for admins. Remove unknown passkeys after a takeover.

decks.title: Know your Java runtime
cards: Know your Java runtime

On 17 November 2026, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) urged immediate patching of a Java flaw, CVE-2026-114938. Run `java -version` to see which Java runtime runs by default on a server. CISA warns that apps and container images can bundle their own Java, so check those too.

decks.title: Leaked keys get used in seconds
cards: Leaked keys get used in seconds

Stony Brook University researchers planted Amazon Web Services (AWS) keys in public container images. The fastest bot used a key 7.86 seconds after it went public. Scan images for secrets before you push them.

decks.title: Spot the mistake: a requirements file
cards: Spot the mistake: a requirements file

A requirements file says `agent-framework>=1.26.0`. The mistake is the loose version rule. For about an hour on 17 November (UTC), it would have installed malicious 1.26.1 or 1.26.2. Pin exact versions: `agent-framework==1.26.0`.

decks.title: Valid logins don't raise alarms
cards: Valid logins don't raise alarms

Uber says 149,346 people had data exposed through stolen credentials at a service provider, Fireworks AI. Uber says it wasn't alerted because the attacker used valid credentials. Watch for unusual use, not only failed logins.

decks.title: Spot the mistake: "Coles was breached"
cards: Spot the mistake: "Coles was breached"

On 16 November 2026, Coles reported a cyber incident to the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX). It says it found no evidence that customer, team member or supplier data was taken. "Incident" isn't the same as a confirmed breach.

decks.title: Ivanti VPN zero-day chain
cards: Key terms

Virtual private network (VPN) appliance: a device that lets staff connect to the internal network from outside.
Zero-day: a flaw attackers use before a fix exists.
Root access: full control of a device.
Web shell: a hidden page an attacker leaves on a server to keep control of it.
What happened

In early October 2026, Volexity caught an attacker it tracks as UTA0576 using zero-days against Ivanti Connect Secure, a virtual private network (VPN) appliance. Ivanti fixed the first flaw, CVE-2026-104935, on 13 October. It fixed two more, CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527, on 29 October.
How they got in

A crafted web request got past the login without an account and led to code execution. The attacker chained two more flaws to get root access, which means full control. The victim's appliance was fully patched at the time, so these were true zero-days.
What the attacker did

The attacker used the appliance's own Active Directory (AD) service account to hunt for stored admin passwords and BitLocker recovery keys. BitLocker is Windows disk encryption, and its recovery keys unlock the disk.
How it stayed hidden
The attacker left no web shell. It re-ran the exploit chain for each command, in memory, and deleted matching log entries. Volexity found Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool showed no changes.
Lesson: patch every round
Upgrade to the fixed build for your branch in Ivanti's advisory, such as 22.8R2.6 or 25.1.1.3. Systems patched on 13 October were still exposed to two more flaws.
Lesson: assume stored secrets are stolen
Volexity advises treating credentials stored on the appliance as stolen and resetting them. Give the VPN's service account only the access it needs.
Lesson: send logs off the box
Send appliance logs to a security information and event management (SIEM) system. Logs kept only on the appliance can be deleted by an attacker who controls it.
decks.maps: A07 Authentication Failures · NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) PR.PS platform security · CSF DE.CM continuous monitoring

q.q: Why might Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool show nothing on a hacked appliance?
o: The attacker deleted the checker tool
The attacker's commands ran only in memory
The attacker encrypted the appliance's disk
q.w: The attacker's commands ran only in memory. Volexity found the tool showed no changes, so memory and network forensics were needed. Not deleting the tool or encrypting the disk: the attacker stayed quiet instead.

decks.entry: A chain of three zero-day flaws in Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliances.
decks.impact: Root access to patched appliances, and a hunt for admin passwords and BitLocker keys.
decks.lesson: Patch every round of fixes. Send appliance logs to a SIEM.

decks.title: Fireworks AI breaches: stolen credentials and a cloud provider
cards: Key terms

Secret: a password, key or token that lets software log in to another service.
Model weights: the learned numbers that make an AI model work.
Third-party provider: an outside company whose service you rely on.
Rotation: replacing a secret with a new one so the old one stops working.
What happened

On 6 October 2026, AI model platform Fireworks AI found someone using its internal credentials without permission. In a 9 November update, it said an attacker had also reached its development machines on 24 October.
How they got in

The first incident used stolen Fireworks credentials. For the second, a third-party cloud provider that hosted Fireworks' research and development machines had its own incident on 23 October. The attacker used that access to reach Fireworks' machines. Fireworks hasn't named the provider.
Impact on Fireworks

In the 24 October activity, the attacker reached customer account and billing information. For some accounts, it also reached stored secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights. Payment card numbers weren't exposed, because Fireworks doesn't store them.
Impact on Uber
Uber named Fireworks AI as the provider in its own breach. Uber says data on 149,346 people, including driver's licence numbers, was stolen through Fireworks.
Where it stands
On 17 November, Fireworks said Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 had finished its investigation of the first incident. It said that incident is contained and fixed.
Lesson: your supplier's suppliers
Your supplier's suppliers are part of your attack surface too. Ask vendors who hosts their systems, and keep development machines away from customer secrets and data.
Lesson: rotate straight away
If a provider says stored secrets may be exposed, rotate every key you kept there straight away. Don't wait to hear whether your account was affected.
decks.maps: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) GV.SC supply chain risk · CSF PR.DS data security · CSF PR.AA identity and access

q.q: A provider says some customers' stored secrets were accessed. You kept an API key there. What's your first move?
o: Rotate the key now
Delete the key from your own notes
Wait until they confirm your account was affected
q.w: Rotate the key now. Once its storage is breached, assume the key is exposed, and rotation makes a stolen copy useless. Not waiting: an attacker can use it meanwhile. Not deleting your notes: the stolen copy still works.

decks.entry: Stolen internal credentials, then access through a third-party cloud provider.
decks.impact: Customer account data and some secrets reached. Uber says 149,346 people's data was taken.
decks.lesson: Rotate secrets as soon as a provider is breached. Know your suppliers' suppliers.
decks.source: Fireworks AI security bulletins, The Record and TechCrunch, 2026

decks.title: Canvas (Instructure) breach hits NZ and AU universities
cards: Key terms

Learning platform: an online system where students get course material and hand in work.
Defacement: changing a website's pages to show the attacker's message.
Extortion: demanding money not to release stolen data.
What happened

In late April and early May 2026, the ShinyHunters group breached Instructure, which makes the Canvas learning platform. Students at the University of Auckland, AUT and Victoria University of Wellington had data exposed. On 7 May the group changed Canvas login pages at about 330 institutions.
How they got in

Instructure said the attacker exploited an issue related to its Free-For-Teacher accounts. These let educators sign up without being verified by a school. Instructure hasn't published technical details, and it has shut the free programme down.
Impact

Instructure said the exposed data likely included names, email addresses, student ID numbers and messages. It said passwords, birthdates, government IDs and financial details weren't believed to be involved. Canvas went offline during assessments, and NZ universities gave students extensions.
The deal with the hackers

In mid-May, Instructure said it had reached an agreement with the hackers. The hackers sent "shred logs" claiming the data was destroyed. Instructure said there's never complete certainty when dealing with cyber criminals.
Lesson: your data at a supplier
The universities' own systems weren't breached, but their students' data still was, because it sat with a supplier. Ask what data your suppliers hold, and how they protect it.
Lesson: free sign-ups are attack surface
A free, unverified sign-up tier lets anyone in. If it shares systems with paying customers, it's part of your attack surface.
decks.maps: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) GV.SC cybersecurity supply chain risk management · CSF RC.CO incident recovery communication

q.q: The hackers sent "shred logs" claiming stolen data was destroyed. What's the safe takeaway?
o: The data is now safe, so no action is needed
Treat the data as exposed anyway
It proves the universities' own servers were hacked
q.w: Treat the data as exposed anyway. Instructure itself said there's never complete certainty, and you can't verify a criminal's promise. Not safe: logs from criminals prove nothing. Not the universities' servers: the breach was at Instructure.

decks.entry: An issue with free, unverified Free-For-Teacher accounts.
decks.impact: Student data from many institutions, including three NZ universities, and defaced login pages.
decks.lesson: Know what data suppliers hold. Treat promises from criminals as worthless.

decks.title: North Korean IT worker hired by an NZ business
cards: Key terms

Remote contractor: someone hired to work from another location, often never met in person.
Identity proofing: checking a person's identity documents are real and belong to them.
Sanctions: legal limits on dealing with a country, such as paying its workers.
What happened

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) NZ released its Cyber Threat Report 2026 on 24 September 2026. It described a large New Zealand business that hired a fake remote IT contractor. The contractor turned out to be a North Korean operative.
How they got in

They got in through hiring, not hacking. The worker used fake identity documents and a New Zealand address as a contact point. A New Zealand citizen was recruited to receive and operate the company's laptop.
Impact

The business grew suspicious and contacted NCSC and NZ Police. It ended the contract and refused to pay. The worker then claimed to hold commercially sensitive information and threatened to release it unless paid.
It's also a sanctions issue
NCSC says paying North Korean workers breaches United Nations (UN) sanctions, which apply under NZ law. So a business can break the law without knowing it.
Lesson: check identity in person
Identity checks are a security control. NCSC suggests interviewing candidates face to face and having new staff pick up IT equipment in person.
decks.maps: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) GV.RR roles and responsibilities · CSF PR.AA identity and access

q.q: Which NCSC NZ tip most directly stops someone else using a new hire's work laptop?
o: Send the laptop by tracked courier
Require longer passwords on the laptop
Make new staff collect IT equipment in person
q.w: Make new staff collect IT equipment in person. In this case a local helper received and ran the laptop. Not a courier: it delivers to whatever address you're given. Not longer passwords: they don't help if the wrong person holds the laptop.

decks.entry: A fake remote contractor hired with false identity documents.
decks.impact: A North Korean operative worked inside the business, then tried extortion.
decks.lesson: Interview face to face. Hand over equipment in person.
decks.source: NCSC NZ Cyber Threat Report 2026, 1News and RNZ

decks.title: Port 445 and the Outlook zero-day
cards: Port 445 and the Outlook zero-day

On 10 November 2026, Microsoft fixed an exploited Outlook flaw, CVE-2026-124194. It can leak NT LAN Manager (NTLM) password hashes. The fix is in the Office updates, not the Windows update. Blocking outbound TCP 445, used by Server Message Block (SMB), cuts off a common path for these leaks.

decks.title: Spot the mistake: "We patched Ivanti in October"
cards: Spot the mistake: "We patched Ivanti in October"

"We installed Ivanti's 13 October fix, so we're safe." The mistake is that two more chained flaws were fixed on 29 October. Builds 22.8R2.5 and 25.1.1.2 are still exposed. Check Ivanti's table for your branch.

decks.title: A clean scan isn't proof
cards: A clean scan isn't proof
In the Ivanti attacks, commands ran in memory and log entries were deleted. Volexity found Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool showed no changes. Investigators needed memory images and crash dumps.

decks.title: AU breach reports, January to June 2026
cards: AU breach reports, January to June 2026
The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) received 667 notifiable data breach notifications from January to June 2026. That's up from 662 in the previous six months.

decks.title: IT support skills that are already security skills
cards: Key terms

Multi-factor authentication (MFA): proving who you are in two different ways, such as a password and an app prompt.
Identity verification: confirming a person is who they say they are before you act.
Identity and access management (IAM): controlling who has an account and what each account can reach.
Incident documentation: a written record of what happened, when, and what was done.
How to use this deck

Each card names a security skill that IT support work often includes. Only use the lines that match work you've really done. Fill each blank with true details, and bring numbers you can explain in an interview.
Identity checks are a security control

If your job includes resetting passwords or MFA, checking the caller's identity first is a security control. Help desks are a social engineering target. MGM Resorts' 2023 breach began with a call to its IT help desk.
CV line: Verified identity before ___ (password resets, MFA changes) using ___ (your process).
Interview line: "Before any ___, I confirmed identity by ___. That helps stop the help desk being the way in."
Account admin is IAM

If your job includes setting up new starters, changing access or removing leavers, that's identity and access management (IAM). The security goal is least privilege: only the access each job needs.
CV line: Managed ___ (new starters, role changes, leavers) in ___ (system), removing leavers' access within ___.
Interview line: "When someone left, I ___ on their last day, so no old account stayed open."
Ticket notes are incident documentation

If your job includes writing ticket notes, you already practise incident documentation. Good security notes record the time, what you saw, what you did and who you told.
CV line: Wrote ticket notes recording ___ (times, evidence, actions) for about ___ tickets a ___.
Interview line: "I wrote notes so ___ could pick up a ticket without asking me. In security, that's the incident timeline."
Reimaging is part of incident recovery

If your job includes wiping and rebuilding infected or broken computers, that's part of incident response. In a security incident, contain it first and keep evidence before wiping. Rebuilding from a clean image is recovery.
CV line: Rebuilt ___ (devices) from a clean image after ___ (malware, faults), restoring users within ___.
Interview line: "If I suspected an attack, I'd isolate the device and escalate before wiping it."
Patching is vulnerability management

If your job includes installing updates or rolling out patches, that's vulnerability management. Security teams prioritise by severity and by whether a flaw is being exploited, using sources such as CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list.
CV line: Kept ___ (devices, apps) patched using ___ (tool), within ___ of release.
Interview line: "I'd patch internet-facing and actively exploited flaws first."
Reported phishing is triage

If your job includes checking suspicious emails users report, deciding what's real is triage, a core security operations centre (SOC) task. Check the sender, the links and whether anyone clicked.
CV line: Checked ___ (number) suspicious emails a ___ and escalated ___ (what).
Interview line: "When a user reported a phish, I ___, then ___."
Backups and restores protect availability

If your job includes checking backups or restoring files, you protect availability, the A in the confidentiality, integrity and availability (CIA) triad. A backup only counts if a restore has been tested.
CV line: Ran ___ (backup checks, test restores) for ___ (systems) every ___.
Interview line: "I don't trust a backup until I've restored from it."
Calm customer service is incident communication

If your job includes calming upset customers and explaining problems simply, that's incident communication. In an incident, people need clear, honest updates.
CV line: Explained ___ (technical issues) to ___ (customers, staff) in plain language.
Interview line: "I'd tell people what we know, what we're doing and when the next update is."
decks.maps: CSF PR.AA identity and access · CSF RS.MA incident management · CSF RC.RP recovery

qs.q: A caller wants an urgent password reset. You ring back on the staff directory number. What control is that?
o: Least privilege
Data loss prevention
Identity verification
qs.w: Identity verification. Calling back on a number you already trust confirms who you're talking to. Not least privilege: that limits access, not who gets it. Not data loss prevention: that stops data leaving.

qs.q: A staff member leaves today. Which identity and access management (IAM) step matters most?
o: Disable their accounts and sign-ins today
Keep the account open for a month, just in case
Copy their access to whoever replaces them
qs.w: Disable their accounts and sign-ins today. Old accounts are a common way in. Not keeping it open: that leaves a working login nobody watches. Not copying access: give the new person only what their job needs.

decks.title: Phish triage: reading email headers
cards: Key terms

Display name: the friendly name shown next to an email address, which the sender can set to anything.
Envelope sender: the sender address given to the receiving server, where bounces go. It's shown as Return-Path, and can differ from the From address.
Reply-To: where your reply goes if you press Reply.
Authentication-Results: a header your mail server adds, showing the results of its sender checks.
From can say anything
The From line has a display name and an address. Anyone can type any display name, such as "IT Service Desk". Read the domain after the @ sign instead.
SPF checks the delivery address
Sender Policy Framework (SPF) checks that the sending server is allowed to send for the envelope sender's domain. That's the Return-Path domain, which can differ from the From address.
DKIM checks a signature
DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) adds a digital signature. A pass means the message wasn't changed after signing, and it was signed by the domain shown as d=.
DMARC ties the checks to From

Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC) passes only if SPF or DKIM passes for a matching domain. The domain must match the From domain, or be a subdomain of it under the usual relaxed setting. This match is called alignment. The domain owner's policy says what to do on a fail: none, quarantine or reject.
Pass doesn't mean safe
An attacker can register a look-alike domain and set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC for it. A pass proves which domain sent the email. It doesn't prove that domain is trustworthy.
Links can lie

Link text can show one address while the link goes to another. On a computer, hover over the link. On a phone, long-press it to see the real address. On an iPhone, tap Hide Preview so the page doesn't load.
Pick the action

Purge removes the email from every mailbox. Block stops the sender or domain. Reset means a new password and revoked sessions, if someone entered credentials. Report tells your security team, and helps catch the next campaign.
decks.maps: CSF DE.AE adverse event analysis · CSF RS.AN incident analysis

qs.q: An email's From address is ceo@ironbark.example, but SPF passed for bulkmailer.example. What decides whether DMARC passes?
o: Whether the Reply-To matches the From address
Whether SPF or DKIM passed for a domain matching ironbark.example
Whether the display name matches the CEO's real name
qs.w: Whether SPF or DKIM passed for a domain matching ironbark.example. DMARC needs alignment with the From domain. Not the Reply-To or display name: DMARC doesn't check either.

qs.q: A reported email passes SPF, DKIM and DMARC. What does that prove?
o: The email is safe to act on
The email came from the domain it shows
Your own IT team sent the email
qs.w: The email came from the domain it shows. Attackers can set up all three checks on a look-alike domain. Not safe: a pass says nothing about intent. Not your IT team: check whether the domain is really yours.

decks.title: Phish triage: password expiry
cards: The evidence
Two staff report this email. Ironbark's real domain is ironbark.example.

qs.q: Which domain really sent this email?
o: ironbark.example
ironbark-it.example
mx.ironbark.example
qs.w: ironbark-it.example, a look-alike. Ironbark only appears in the display name and link text, and mx.ironbark.example is your own mail server.

qs.q: All three checks pass. What does that prove?
o: It's genuine, so it's safe to act on
Ironbark's own IT team sent it out
It came from ironbark-it.example
qs.w: It came from ironbark-it.example. The attacker set up the checks on their own look-alike domain. A pass proves the domain, not that it's yours or safe.

qs.q: What gives the link away?
o: The address starts with HTTPS
The link sits in the middle of the body
Its text and real address differ
qs.w: Its text and real address differ: it shows login.ironbark.example but goes to ironbark-it.example. Not HTTPS: phishing sites use it too. Not its place in the body: real emails have links there too.

qs.q: One user entered their password on the fake page. Best response?
o: Warn all staff, then wait
Reset every staff password
Purge, block, reset and revoke
qs.w: Purge, block the domain, then reset that user and revoke sessions. Only one user entered a password, and the attacker can log in now.

after: Check for persistence
After a password is stolen, check that user's account for new inbox forwarding rules and new MFA methods. Attackers add these to keep access after a reset.

decks.title: Phish triage: a request from the CEO
cards: The evidence
The accounts team reports this business email compromise (BEC) attempt. CEO Sarah Chen's real address is sarah.chen@ironbark.example.

From: "Sarah Chen"
  <sarah.chen.ironbark@freemail.example>
Reply-To: s.chen.office@freemail.example
Subject: Quick favour, confidential
Authentication-Results:
  spf=pass dkim=pass dmarc=pass
  header.from=freemail.example
Body: In meetings all day. Buy 5 x $200
  gift cards and email me the codes.
  Keep it between us.

qs.q: Who really sent this email?
o: Ironbark's own mail server, mx.ironbark.example
Sarah Chen, from her Ironbark work account
Someone on a free email account
qs.w: Someone on a free email account: the domain is freemail.example. Only the display name says Sarah Chen. Your mail server only received the email.

qs.q: What's suspicious about the Reply-To?
o: It matches the From address exactly
It's missing, so replies go nowhere
It sends replies to another address
qs.w: It sends replies to another address the scammer controls, s.chen.office@freemail.example. It's there, and it differs from the From address.

qs.q: What should the accounts team do?
o: Reply and ask whether it's really her
Buy the cards but keep all the receipts
Call her directory number, then report it
qs.w: Call her directory number, then report it. Replying reaches the scammer. Money sent as gift card codes is rarely recovered.

after: Why there's no link
BEC emails often have no link or attachment, so filters have little to catch. Urgency, secrecy and a payment request are the warning signs.

decks.title: Phish triage: payroll bank details
cards: The evidence

Payroll reports an email asking staff to update bank details. Sender Policy Framework (SPF) checks Return-Path. Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC) ties the checks to From.

qs.q: SPF passed. Why did DMARC fail?
o: DMARC also needs a signature check
SPF passed for a different domain
The Reply-To was a free account
qs.w: SPF passed for bulkmailer.example, which doesn't match From. An aligned SPF pass alone would have been enough. DMARC doesn't check Reply-To.

qs.q: DMARC failed, but the email still arrived. Why?
o: The fail was a mistake by the mail server
SPF overrides DMARC when SPF passes
Ironbark's DMARC policy is set to none
qs.w: The policy is none, so receivers only monitor: that's what action=none shows. The fail was correct, and SPF can't override DMARC.

qs.q: What's the best response?
o: Reply to the sender to confirm the change
Reset the payroll team's passwords today
Purge, block the senders, tighten DMARC
qs.w: Purge it, block the senders, and move DMARC to quarantine or reject. Replying reaches the scammer. No login was stolen, so password resets don't help.

after: Close the gap

With a DMARC policy of quarantine or reject, receivers would have sent this email to junk or refused it. Move to it gradually: watch the DMARC reports first so your own real senders don't get blocked.

decks.title: Phish triage: a contract to sign
cards: The evidence
m.lee reports this email. Ironbark uses SignFlow, and facilities sent a lease for signing today.

qs.q: Is this email phishing?
o: Yes, because it contains a link to sign
Yes, because it's from an outside company
Probably not: everything matches
qs.w: Probably not: the sender, link and context all match, and all three checks pass. Many genuine emails have links and come from outside companies.

qs.q: What should you do?
o: Block signflow.example for everyone
Purge it from every mailbox right away
Tell m.lee it's genuine, with thanks
qs.w: Tell m.lee it's genuine and thank them. Blocking or purging would stop real business. Thanks keep people reporting.

after: Not every report is phish
Part of triage is saying "this one's fine" quickly and clearly. Treating every report as an attack wastes time and frustrates the business.

decks.title: NZISM and the PSR
cards: Key terms

NZISM: the New Zealand Information Security Manual, the government's manual for protecting information and systems.
Protective Security Requirements (PSR): the government's wider security framework, covering people, information and physical security.
Control: a specific safeguard, such as patching or logging.
What the NZISM is

The New Zealand Information Security Manual (NZISM) is the government's manual for information security. It's published by the Government Communications Security Bureau (GCSB) through the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC). Version 3.9, from April 2025, is current.
MUST and SHOULD
NZISM controls use the words MUST and SHOULD. A MUST is required. A SHOULD is strongly recommended, and an agency that doesn't follow it needs to record why.
What the PSR is

The Protective Security Requirements (PSR) set out how the New Zealand government expects agencies to manage security. They cover four areas: security governance, information security, personnel security and physical security.
How they fit together
The NZISM sits under the information security part of the PSR. The PSR sets the overall expectations, and the NZISM gives the detailed technical controls.
Who must follow them
The PSR's requirements are mandatory for certain government agencies, and they assess themselves against them every year. For other organisations, the PSR and NZISM are best practice.
Why it matters for your job hunt
Government agencies and their IT suppliers are big employers of security staff in New Zealand. Knowing what the NZISM and PSR are is a quick way to stand out in those interviews.
decks.maps: Security+ Security Program Management and Oversight · NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) GV.PO policy

q.q: An NZISM control says an agency SHOULD do something. What does that mean?
o: Optional, and nothing needs recording
Required, with no exceptions allowed
Recommended; skipping needs a reason
q.w: Recommended; skipping it needs a recorded reason. Not required with no exceptions: that's what MUST means. Not optional with no record: an agency has to justify not following a SHOULD.

decks.title: NCSC NZ: who they are and how to report
cards: Key terms

National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC): New Zealand's lead government agency for cyber security, part of the GCSB.
CERT NZ: the agency that used to take incident reports, now merged into the NCSC.
Incident of potential national significance: an incident serious enough for the NCSC's specialist help.
One place to report
The integration of CERT NZ into the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) was completed on 23 July 2025. Individuals, businesses and critical infrastructure now report cyber incidents in one place.
How to report
Report online at ncsc.govt.nz, or call the NCSC on 0800 114 115. The old CERT NZ website has been retired. Own Your Online still gives advice for individuals and small businesses.
The 2024/25 numbers
The Cyber Threat Report 2025 covers 1 July 2024 to 30 June 2025. It received 5,995 reports. It handled 331 incidents of potential national significance, down from 343 the year before.
How bad it got in 2024/25
The NCSC rates incidents from C1, a national cyber emergency, down to C6. In 2024/25, the most severe incidents were rated C3. None reached C1.
The first C2s in years

In the first quarter of 2026, the NCSC recorded three C2, or highly significant, incidents. They were the first since 2021/22. The NCSC said basics such as MFA and protecting network edges could have helped.
The 2025/26 picture
The Cyber Threat Report 2026, released on 24 September 2026, covers 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026. The NCSC handled 369 incidents of potential national significance, up from 331. Four were rated C2.
decks.maps: CSF RS.CO incident response reporting and communication

q.q: Since July 2025, where does a New Zealand business report a cyber incident?
o: CERT NZ's own website
The Privacy Commissioner only
The NCSC, online or by phone
q.w: The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), online or on 0800 114 115. Not CERT NZ: it merged into the NCSC and its website was retired. Not only the Privacy Commissioner: a notifiable privacy breach goes there too, but that's a separate duty.

decks.title: NZ privacy principles for security staff
cards: Key terms

Information privacy principle (IPP): one of the rules in New Zealand's Privacy Act 2020 for handling personal information.
Personal information: information about an identifiable person.
Serious harm: the test for whether a privacy breach must be reported.
The principles
The Privacy Act 2020 has 13 information privacy principles (IPPs). A 14th, IPP 3A, came into force on 1 May 2026. It covers telling people when you collect their information from someone else.
IPP 5: keep it secure

IPP 5 says an organisation must protect personal information with reasonable security safeguards. It must protect against loss, misuse and unauthorised access. This is the principle security teams work on every day.
IPP 9: don't keep it too long
IPP 9 says don't keep personal information longer than you need it. Data you no longer hold can't be stolen. The Latitude breach in 2023 exposed records that hadn't been needed for years.
IPP 11 and 12: sharing
IPP 11 limits when you can disclose personal information. IPP 12 limits sending it overseas. Usually, the receiver must protect it to a similar standard.
Notifiable privacy breaches

A privacy breach that has caused, or is likely to cause, serious harm must be reported. Tell the Privacy Commissioner and affected people as soon as practicable. Failing to notify the Commissioner is an offence, with a fine up to NZ$10,000.
decks.maps: Security+ Security Program Management and Oversight · NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) GV.OC legal requirements

q.q: A company keeps closed customers' licence numbers "just in case". Which principle is it most likely breaking?
o: IPP 5: security safeguards
IPP 9: retention
IPP 12: overseas disclosure
q.w: IPP 9: retention. Information should only be kept as long as it's needed. Not IPP 5: the data may be well protected, but it shouldn't be there. Not IPP 12: nothing is being sent overseas.

decks.title: Mercury IT ransomware
cards: Key terms

Managed service provider (MSP): a company that runs IT systems for other organisations.
Ransomware: malware that locks files and demands payment.
Coronial file: a record about a death investigated by a coroner.
What happened
