In late November 2022, ransomware hit Mercury IT, a Wellington managed service provider (MSP). The attack spread to the data of several of its clients. The Privacy Commissioner was told on 30 November, and it became public on 6 December.
Who was affected

The Ministry of Justice said about 14,500 coronial files and about 4,000 post-mortem reports were affected. Te Whatu Ora (Health New Zealand) lost access to some health records. The health insurer Accuro was also affected.
The response
The High Court ordered that nobody may store, publish, share or access files stolen in the attack. In December 2022, the Privacy Commissioner opened a compliance investigation.
Lesson: your supplier holds your data
None of these agencies ran Mercury IT's systems, but their data sat there. Ask what data your suppliers hold, how they protect it, and how fast they'll tell you about a breach.
Lesson: one supplier, many victims
Attacking one supplier can reach many organisations at once. That makes managed service providers a favourite target, and a key part of supply chain risk.
decks.maps: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) RS.MA incident management · Privacy Act 2020 IPP 5 security safeguards

q.q: Why did one attack on Mercury IT affect several government agencies at once?
o: The agencies shared one password
The agencies' data sat with the same provider
The attack spread through the government network
q.w: The agencies' data sat with the same provider. Attacking one supplier reached all of them. Not a shared password or the government network: the attack was on Mercury IT's own systems.

decks.entry: Ransomware at Mercury IT, a Wellington managed service provider. How it got in hasn't been made public.
decks.impact: About 14,500 coronial files and 4,000 post-mortem reports affected, plus health and insurance data.
decks.lesson: Know which suppliers hold your data, and check how they protect it.
decks.source: Ministry of Justice and the Privacy Commissioner, 2022

decks.title: Latitude: the New Zealand side
cards: Key terms

Data retention: how long an organisation keeps information.
Joint investigation: two regulators investigating the same breach together.
Gem Visa and Genoapay: Latitude's consumer finance brands in New Zealand.
What happened

In March 2023, attackers stole about 14 million records from Latitude Financial, which runs Gem Visa and Genoapay in New Zealand. Latitude's systems were breached through a vendor's login. It was New Zealand's biggest data breach.
The New Zealand impact

The Privacy Commissioner said over one million past and present New Zealand driver licence numbers were exposed, as well as passport details. Many belonged to people who hadn't been customers for years.
Replacing licences
Waka Kotahi, the NZ Transport Agency, made it easier for affected people to replace their driver licence. A stolen licence number can be used in identity fraud.
A first for two regulators

On 9 May 2023, New Zealand's Privacy Commissioner and Australia's privacy regulator opened their first joint investigation. It covers how Latitude protected data, and why it kept data it no longer needed.
Lesson: retention is a security risk
The Deputy Privacy Commissioner called data retention "the sleeping giant of data security". Delete personal information you no longer need. Data you don't hold can't be stolen.
decks.maps: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) GV.SC supply chain risk · Privacy Act 2020 IPP 5 security safeguards

q.q: Which control would most have reduced how many people the Latitude breach hit?
o: Shorter data retention
Longer customer passwords
Encrypting data in transit
q.w: Shorter data retention. Many records belonged to people who hadn't been customers for years. Not longer passwords: customers' passwords weren't how attackers got in. Not encryption in transit: the data was taken from storage.

decks.entry: Attackers used a vendor's login to reach Latitude's systems.
decks.impact: About 14 million records, including over one million NZ driver licence numbers.
decks.lesson: Delete data you no longer need. Retention is a security risk.

decks.title: NZX DDoS attacks
cards: Key terms

Distributed denial of service (DDoS): flooding a service with traffic from many machines so it stops working.
Market announcement: a public notice a listed company must publish, such as its results.
Failover: switching to a backup system when the main one fails.
What happened
In late August 2020, distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks hit NZX, New Zealand's stock exchange. Trading was halted for about four days, with only short periods when it worked.
Why trading stopped
The attacks took down NZX's announcements platform. Companies couldn't publish market announcements, so fair trading wasn't possible, and NZX halted the market.
What the regulator found

In January 2021, the Financial Markets Authority (FMA) said the attack was foreseeable and should have been planned for. Government agencies had warned about such attacks in November 2019. It called NZX's crisis planning "basic".
What NZX changed
NZX didn't accept all the findings. It promised fixes, including a cloud-based failover site for its announcements platform and DDoS protection from Akamai.
Lesson: plan for availability attacks
DDoS attacks don't steal data, but they can stop a business completely. Plan for them before they happen, with protection services and a tested backup.
decks.maps: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) PR.IR technology resilience · CSF RC.RP recovery planning

q.q: Which part of the CIA triad did the NZX attacks mainly hit?
o: Integrity
Availability
Confidentiality
q.w: Availability. Traffic floods stopped the exchange working for about four days. Not confidentiality: no data was reported stolen. Not integrity: data wasn't changed.

decks.entry: Large DDoS traffic floods against NZX's network and announcements platform.
decks.impact: Trading halted for about four days.
decks.lesson: Plan for DDoS before it happens. Test failover.

decks.title: Reading Entra sign-in logs
cards: Key terms

Sign-in log: Microsoft Entra ID's record of each attempt to sign in.
Interactive sign-in: one where a person types a password or approves a prompt.
Non-interactive sign-in: one an app does for a user in the background, such as refreshing a token.
Error code: a number showing why a sign-in failed.
Four kinds of sign-in

Microsoft Entra ID logs four kinds of sign-in: interactive user, non-interactive user, service principal (an app's own identity) and managed identity. Check all four. An attacker with a stolen token can show up only as non-interactive sign-ins.
What each entry shows

Each sign-in shows the user, the app, the internet (IP) address, the location and the device. It also shows whether multi-factor authentication (MFA) was needed, which Conditional Access policies applied, and whether the attempt succeeded.
Error codes to know
50126 means a wrong username or password. 50053 means the account is locked, or the sign-in came from a known bad IP. 53003 means Conditional Access blocked it. 500121 means the MFA step failed.
How long logs last
Sign-in logs are kept for 7 days on Entra ID Free, and 30 days with Entra ID P1 or P2. To keep them longer, send them to a Log Analytics workspace or Microsoft Sentinel.
Spotting a password spray
A password spray shows as many 50126 failures across many accounts, often from one IP address or a few. Then look for any success from the same address.
decks.maps: SC-200 respond to incidents · SC-900 Microsoft Entra · NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) DE.CM continuous monitoring

qs.q: An Entra sign-in shows error code 53003. What happened?
o: The password was wrong
The MFA step failed
Conditional Access blocked it
qs.w: Conditional Access blocked it: 53003 means a policy stopped the sign-in. Not a wrong password: that's 50126. Not a failed MFA step: that's 500121.

qs.q: You have Entra ID P1 and send sign-in logs to Sentinel. A user asks about a sign-in from 45 days ago. Where do you look?
o: The Entra sign-in logs page
The Windows Security event log
Sentinel or Log Analytics
qs.w: Sentinel or Log Analytics, if you send sign-in logs there. Entra keeps them for 30 days with P1, so 45 days needs a longer store. Not the Windows Security log: cloud sign-ins aren't recorded there.

decks.title: Intune and Conditional Access
cards: Key terms

Microsoft Intune: Microsoft's service for managing and securing devices.
Compliance policy: the rules a device must meet, such as encryption or a minimum operating system version.
Conditional Access: Entra ID policies that decide whether a sign-in is allowed, and under what conditions.
Compliance policies

Microsoft Intune checks enrolled devices against compliance policies. A policy might require BitLocker disk encryption, a minimum Windows version, a screen lock and an up-to-date antivirus. Each device is then marked compliant or not compliant.
Linking it to Conditional Access
Conditional Access can use that result. A grant control called "Require device to be marked as compliant" lets only compliant devices reach the app. Everything else is blocked.
Why it matters
A stolen password alone isn't enough if Conditional Access also needs a compliant device. The attacker's own laptop isn't enrolled in Intune, so it can't be marked compliant.
Grace periods
Compliance policies can give a device time to fix a problem before it's marked not compliant. This stops people being locked out the moment an update is due.
Test before you enforce
Run a new Conditional Access policy in report-only mode first. It logs what would have happened without blocking anyone. Keep break-glass accounts excluded, so a mistake can't lock out every admin.
decks.maps: SC-900 Microsoft Entra · SC-200 manage a security operations environment · NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) PR.AA identity and access

qs.q: An attacker has a user's password and MFA approval but uses their own laptop. Which control blocks the sign-in?
o: A longer password policy
Require a compliant device
Self-service password reset
qs.w: Require a compliant device. The attacker's laptop isn't enrolled in Intune, so it can't be marked compliant. Not a longer password: they already have it. Not self-service reset: that helps users, not blocking.

decks.title: Defender for Office 365
cards: Key terms

Safe Links: checks a link when someone clicks it, not only when the email arrives.
Safe Attachments: opens attachments in a separate safe environment to check them before delivery.
Quarantine: a holding area for suspicious emails.
Message trace: a search that shows where an email went.
Safe Links
Safe Links checks links (URLs) at the moment someone clicks them, in email and Office apps. That matters because attackers often make a link harmful only after the email is delivered.
Safe Attachments
Safe Attachments opens attachments in a separate virtual environment to watch what they do. Malicious ones are blocked before they reach the user.
Quarantine

Suspicious emails can be held in quarantine. Quarantine policies decide whether users can release their own messages. By default, only admins can release emails quarantined as high-confidence phishing.
Zero-hour auto purge
Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) removes emails after delivery when they're later found to be malicious. It's one reason a reported phish may already be gone.
Message trace

Message trace, in the Exchange admin centre, shows whether an email was delivered, filtered as spam or quarantined, and to whom. It covers the last 90 days, searched up to 10 days at a time. Use it to find everyone who got a phish.
decks.maps: SC-900 Microsoft security solutions · SC-200 respond to incidents · NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) PR.PS platform security

qs.q: A link in an email was safe when it arrived but turned malicious an hour later. Which feature still protects a user who clicks it?
o: Message trace
Safe Links
Safe Attachments
qs.w: Safe Links, because it checks the URL at the moment of the click. Not Safe Attachments: it checks files, not links. Not message trace: it shows where emails went but blocks nothing.

qs.q: You need to know which staff received a phishing email. Which tool shows that?
o: Quarantine
Message trace
Safe Attachments
qs.w: Message trace shows each email's recipients and whether it was delivered. Not quarantine: it only holds emails that were caught. Not Safe Attachments: it scans files.

decks.title: Purview labels and DLP
cards: Key terms

Microsoft Purview: Microsoft's tools for protecting and governing data.
Sensitivity label: a tag on a file or email, such as Confidential, that can also apply protection.
Data loss prevention (DLP): rules that spot sensitive information and stop it being shared in risky ways.
Sensitivity labels

A sensitivity label, such as Public or Confidential, marks how sensitive a file or email is. A label can also add encryption, a header or a watermark. The protection stays with the file wherever it goes.
Applying labels
People can apply labels themselves, or labels can be suggested or applied automatically when sensitive content is found. Automatic labelling needs higher-tier licences.
Data loss prevention
Data loss prevention (DLP) policies look for sensitive information types, such as credit card numbers. When they find them, they can show a warning tip, block sharing or alert an admin.
New Zealand patterns
Purview includes New Zealand sensitive information types. They include bank account numbers, driver licence numbers, Inland Revenue (IRD) numbers and Ministry of Health (NHI) numbers.
Start in test mode
Run a new DLP policy in simulation mode first and review the matches. Blocking too much stops real work, and people start finding workarounds.
decks.maps: SC-900 Microsoft compliance solutions · Security+ Security Architecture · NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) PR.DS data security

qs.q: Staff keep emailing spreadsheets of customer IRD numbers to personal accounts. What helps most?
o: A Safe Links policy for IRD numbers
A sensitivity label for IRD numbers
A DLP policy for IRD numbers
qs.w: A DLP policy for IRD numbers can spot them and block or warn on sharing. Not a label alone: it marks the file but doesn't stop sharing by itself. Not Safe Links: it checks links, not attachments.

qs.q: A label adds encryption to a file. A staff member emails it outside the company. What happens to the protection?
o: The label is removed on sending
The file is blocked from sending
The protection stays with the file
qs.w: The protection stays with the file wherever it goes, so only permitted people can open it. Not removed: labels travel with the file. Not blocked: that would need a DLP policy.

qs.q: Why run a new DLP policy in simulation mode first?
o: To make the policy run faster
To review matches before blocking
To stop it alerting admins
qs.w: To review matches before blocking, so real work isn't stopped by mistake. Not speed: simulation doesn't change performance. Not stopping admin alerts: simulation is about checking matches safely.

decks.title: Hunt: a password spray
cards: Key terms

Advanced hunting: writing KQL queries over Microsoft Defender XDR data.
IdentityLogonEvents: a table of sign-ins seen by Defender for Identity and Defender for Cloud Apps.
dcount(): counts distinct values, such as how many different accounts.
Password spray: a few common passwords tried against many accounts.
The query
This Kusto Query Language (KQL) query looks for one IP address failing to sign in to many accounts. That's the pattern of a password spray.

IdentityLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType == "LogonFailed"
| summarize Failures = count(),
    Accounts = dcount(AccountUpn) by IPAddress
| where Accounts > 10
| sort by Failures desc
Why dcount
count() gives total failures, which brute force against one account also produces. dcount(AccountUpn) counts different accounts, which is what separates a spray from one person mistyping.
What to do next
Take the top IP addresses and look for any LogonSuccess from them. A success after a spray means a guessed password worked.
decks.maps: SC-200 perform threat hunting · ATT&CK T1110.003 Password Spraying

qs.q: Why does the query count distinct accounts per IP address?
o: To count total failures
To find the newest failures
To tell a spray from a typo
qs.w: To tell a spray from a typo. One IP failing on many different accounts is a spray. Not total failures: count() already does that. Not the newest: the query doesn't sort by time.

decks.title: Hunt: who got the phish?
cards: Key terms

EmailEvents: an advanced hunting table of emails processed by Microsoft 365.
DeliveryAction: what happened to the email, such as Delivered, Junked or Blocked.
project: a KQL step that keeps only the columns you list.
The query
A user reports a phish from ironbark-it.example. This Kusto Query Language (KQL) query finds everyone else who got email from that domain.

EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where SenderFromDomain ==
    "ironbark-it.example"
| project Timestamp, RecipientEmailAddress,
    Subject, DeliveryAction
Reading the results
Rows with DeliveryAction "Delivered" reached inboxes when they arrived. LatestDeliveryAction shows whether zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) or an admin removed them later. Purge any copies still there.
What to do next
Purge the delivered copies, block the domain, then check whether any recipient clicked. The UrlClickEvents table records clicks on links checked by Safe Links.
decks.maps: SC-200 perform threat hunting · SC-200 respond to incidents

qs.q: Which column tells you whether each copy of the phish reached the inbox?
o: Subject
DeliveryAction
RecipientEmailAddress
qs.w: DeliveryAction shows Delivered, Junked or Blocked. Not Subject: it shows what the email says, not what happened to it. Not RecipientEmailAddress: it says who, not what happened.

decks.title: Hunt: PowerShell on the web
cards: Key terms

DeviceNetworkEvents: an advanced hunting table of network connections from devices with Defender for Endpoint.
InitiatingProcessFileName: the program that made the connection.
Download cradle: a short command that downloads code and runs it straight away.
pwsh.exe: PowerShell 7. Windows PowerShell 5.1 is powershell.exe.
The query
This Kusto Query Language (KQL) query lists web connections made by PowerShell in the last day.

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~
    ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| where RemotePort in (80, 443)
| summarize Connections = count()
    by DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
Why in~
in~ checks a value against a list, without caring about upper or lower case. Process names can appear as PowerShell.exe or powershell.exe, so a case-sensitive match could miss some.
Reading the results
Admin scripts and updates reach known company and Microsoft addresses. A user's laptop reaching a rare domain, or a raw IP address with no RemoteUrl, is worth a closer look.
decks.maps: SC-200 perform threat hunting · ATT&CK T1059.001 PowerShell · ATT&CK T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer

qs.q: Why does the query use in~ instead of in?
o: To match partial file names
To ignore upper and lower case
To require an exact-case match
qs.w: To ignore upper and lower case, so PowerShell.exe and powershell.exe both match. Not partial names: only the two listed names match. Not exact case: that's what in does without the tilde.

decks.title: What's the difference between authentication and authorisation?
decks.answer:
Authentication proves who you are, such as a password plus a multi-factor authentication (MFA) prompt. Authorisation decides what you can do once you're in, such as which folders you can open. Authentication happens first. Authorisation should be checked on every request.
Interviewers listen for: a clear one-line definition of each, a real example, and that authorisation is checked every time. Broken Access Control is A01 in the OWASP Top 10:2025.

decks.title: Walk me through what happens when you type a website address into a browser.
decks.answer:
The browser asks the Domain Name System (DNS) for the site's IP address. It opens a TCP connection to port 443, or uses QUIC over UDP for HTTP/3. Transport Layer Security (TLS) checks the server's certificate and agrees encryption keys. Then the browser sends an HTTP request and shows the page it gets back.
Interviewers listen for: DNS, the connection, the certificate check and the HTTP request, in that order. Bonus: where attacks fit, such as DNS spoofing or a fake certificate.

decks.title: What is the CIA triad? Give an example of an attack on each part.
decks.answer:
Confidentiality means only the right people see data. A data leak breaks it. Integrity means data isn't changed without permission. Tampering with payment details breaks it. Availability means systems work when needed. A denial-of-service attack breaks it.
Interviewers listen for: a definition and an attack for each. Bonus: ransomware with double extortion hits all three.

decks.title: What's the difference between encryption and hashing?
decks.answer:
Encryption is two-way: with the right key, you get the original data back. Hashing is one-way: it makes a fixed-length fingerprint you can't reverse. Use encryption for data you need to read later. Store passwords with slow, salted hashes such as bcrypt or Argon2.
Interviewers listen for: reversible versus one-way, and that passwords are hashed, not encrypted. Bonus: a salt stops identical passwords having identical hashes.

decks.title: What's the difference between a vulnerability, a threat and a risk?
decks.answer:
A vulnerability is a weakness, such as an unpatched VPN. A threat is something that could exploit it, such as a ransomware gang. Risk combines how likely that is with how bad the impact would be. You lower risk by fixing the weakness or reducing the impact.
Interviewers listen for: three separate definitions with one example tying them together, and risk as likelihood and impact.

decks.title: What is phishing-resistant MFA, and why does it matter?
decks.answer:
Phishing-resistant MFA can't be handed over to a fake website. FIDO2 security keys and passkeys are bound to the real site's domain, so a look-alike site gets nothing it can use. Certificate-based smart cards count too. SMS and app codes can be typed into a fake page and replayed straight away.
Interviewers listen for: why codes can be phished, the domain binding, and real examples. Bonus: Cloudflare's staff used FIDO2 keys and blocked the 2022 SMS phishing campaign that hit Twilio.

decks.title: What's the difference between TCP and UDP? Name a security-relevant port for each.
decks.answer:
TCP sets up a connection with a three-way handshake and makes sure data arrives in order. UDP just sends, with no handshake, so it's faster but easier to spoof. SSH uses TCP 22 and Remote Desktop uses TCP 3389. DNS mostly uses UDP 53, and uses TCP for large responses.
Interviewers listen for: handshake versus none, reliability versus speed, and correct port numbers.

decks.title: What does least privilege mean, and how would you apply it in Microsoft 365 or AWS?
decks.answer:
Least privilege means giving each person and process only the access their job needs, for only as long as they need it. In Microsoft 365, use a narrow role such as Helpdesk Administrator instead of Global Administrator. Privileged Identity Management (PIM) can make admin roles time-limited. In AWS, allow specific actions on specific resources, not a wildcard that allows everything.
Interviewers listen for: the definition, one concrete example, and regular access reviews.

decks.title: Which Windows Event IDs would you check for a suspected brute-force attack?
decks.answer:
Event ID 4625 is a failed logon. Many from one source in a short time suggests brute force. Event ID 4624 is a successful logon, which matters most if it comes right after the failures. Event ID 4740 means an account was locked out. The logon type shows how: 3 is network and 10 is Remote Desktop. With Network Level Authentication (NLA) on, failed Remote Desktop logons usually show as type 3.
Interviewers listen for: 4625, a 4624 after the failures, and grouping by account and source IP. Bonus: a password spray is a few tries across many accounts.

decks.title: What is the shared responsibility model in the cloud?
decks.answer:
The cloud provider secures the cloud itself: data centres, hardware and the core services. You secure what you put in it: your data, identities, access settings and configuration. How much is yours depends on the service. You manage much more with a virtual machine than with Microsoft 365.
Interviewers listen for: the split, how it changes between service types, and that most cloud breaches come from the customer's side, such as public storage.

decks.title: A user says their mouse is moving by itself. What do you do, in order?
decks.answer:
First, check whether someone in IT is remotely supporting them. If not, ask the user to stop using the computer but leave it on. Disconnect it from the network, or isolate it with your endpoint detection and response (EDR) tool. Escalate to security, noting the time and what the user saw. Then reset the user's passwords from a clean device.
Interviewers listen for: ruling out legitimate remote support, isolating without powering off so memory evidence survives, escalating, and writing down times.

decks.title: You find a public Amazon S3 bucket with customer data in it. What do you do first?
decks.answer:
Confirm it's your organisation's bucket and what data is in it. Block public access straight away, ideally with S3 Block Public Access. Tell your manager or security team, and record what you did and when. Then check access logs or CloudTrail data events, if they were on, to see who read it.
Interviewers listen for: contain first, keep the evidence, escalate, and check whether it's a notifiable privacy breach that's likely to cause serious harm.

decks.title: A user clicked a phishing link and entered their password. Walk me through your response.
decks.answer:
Reset the password and revoke all active sessions, so stolen session cookies stop working. Check sign-in logs for logins from new places since the click. Look for changes an attacker might have made, such as inbox forwarding rules or new MFA methods. Remove the email from every mailbox and block the sender. Thank the user for reporting it.
Interviewers listen for: revoking sessions, not only resetting the password, checking for persistence, and finding other people who clicked.

decks.title: An alert shows a sign-in from Auckland, then one from overseas 10 minutes later. What do you check?
decks.answer:
First, check whether it's really two places. A VPN or a mobile network can make one person look overseas. Compare the device, browser and IP address for each sign-in, and whether MFA was passed. Contact the user through a channel you already trust. If it isn't them, revoke sessions, reset the password and check for new inbox rules or MFA methods.
Interviewers listen for: considering a false positive, using evidence, verifying the user safely, then responding.

decks.title: A manager asks you to give a new starter the same access as another staff member. What do you do?
decks.answer:
Avoid copying one person's access to another, because it carries over permissions the new starter may not need. Ask what the role needs, or use a group built for that role. Get approval from the right person and record it in the ticket. Set a review date for anything temporary.
Interviewers listen for: least privilege, approval, documentation, and an awareness of access creep, where access builds up over time.

decks.title: Ransom notes appear on a file server. What are your first steps?
decks.answer:
Isolate the affected systems from the network, but don't power them off, so evidence in memory survives. Escalate straight away and follow the incident response plan. Check that backups are offline and unaffected. Record what you see, such as the ransom note, file extensions and times. Leave any contact with the attackers to leadership and legal advisers. Report the incident to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC).
Interviewers listen for: isolate without powering off, escalate, protect backups, keep evidence, and report.

decks.title: A caller says they're the CFO and needs an urgent MFA reset. What do you do?
decks.answer:
Follow the identity check process, even for senior people. Urgent pressure is a classic social engineering sign. Call back on the number in the staff directory, not one the caller gives, or confirm through their manager. If you can't verify them, don't reset anything, and report the call to security.
Interviewers listen for: verifying through a channel you already trust, holding firm under pressure, and reporting. Bonus: MGM Resorts' 2023 breach began with a call to its IT help desk.

decks.title: You see PowerShell running an encoded command on a workstation. How do you investigate?
decks.answer:
Decode the -EncodedCommand value first: it's Base64 of UTF-16LE text. Check what launched PowerShell, such as Word or a scheduled task. Read the full script in Script Block Logging, Event ID 4104, if it's on. Look for network connections and files it created. If it's malicious, isolate the host and check other computers for the same command.
Interviewers listen for: decoding, the parent process, Event ID 4104, containment, and scoping across other machines.

decks.title: Tell me about a time you made a mistake at work.
decks.answer:
There's no model answer: this has to be your own story.
Situation: where you were and what was going on.
Task: what you were responsible for.
Action: what you did when you noticed the mistake, step by step. Say "I", not "we".
Result: what you fixed, and what you now do differently.
Interviewers listen for: honesty, owning it quickly, telling the right people, and a lasting change.
Common mistake: picking a fake mistake, such as "I work too hard". Pick a real, small one you fixed.

decks.title: Tell me about a time you explained something technical to a non-technical person.
decks.answer:
There's no model answer: this has to be your own story.
Situation: who the person was and what they needed to understand.
Task: why it mattered that they understood.
Action: how you explained it. Did you use an everyday comparison, avoid jargon or check they'd understood?
Result: what they could do afterwards.
Interviewers listen for: plain language, patience, and checking understanding. Security analysts explain risk to managers all the time.
Common mistake: describing the technology instead of how you adapted to the person.

decks.title: Tell me about a time you handled a difficult or upset customer.
decks.answer:
There's no model answer: this has to be your own story.
Situation: what the customer was upset about.
Task: what you needed to sort out.
Action: what you said and did, including how you stayed calm.
Result: how it ended, and the customer's reaction if you know it.
Interviewers listen for: calm under pressure, listening, and following process while still helping. This maps well to talking to stressed users during an incident.
Common mistake: blaming the customer. Keep the focus on what you did.

decks.title: Tell me about a time you had several urgent tasks at once. How did you prioritise?
decks.answer:
There's no model answer: this has to be your own story.
Situation: what was competing for your time.
Task: what had to get done, and by when.
Action: how you decided the order, such as by business impact or how many people were affected, and who you told.
Result: what got done, and what you'd change.
Interviewers listen for: a clear way of deciding, communicating delays, and asking for help when needed. Security teams triage alerts the same way.
Common mistake: saying you just worked harder, with no method.

decks.title: Tell me about a time you learned a new technical skill quickly.
decks.answer:
There's no model answer: this has to be your own story.
Situation: what you needed to learn, and why.
Task: how quickly you needed it.
Action: how you learned it, such as documentation, labs or asking a colleague.
Result: what you could do afterwards, with something specific.
Interviewers listen for: a learning method you can repeat, and initiative. Your lab work and certification study count.
Common mistake: listing courses without saying what you can now actually do.

decks.title: Tell me about a time you spotted a problem before it became bigger.
decks.answer:
There's no model answer: this has to be your own story.
Situation: what you noticed, and where.
Task: why it mattered.
Action: what you checked, and who you told.
Result: what was prevented, with a number if you have one.
Interviewers listen for: attention to detail, curiosity, and escalating at the right time. That's the core of security monitoring.
Common mistake: skipping the evidence. Say what made you suspicious.

decks.title: Tell me about a time you followed a process even though it was inconvenient.
decks.answer:
There's no model answer: this has to be your own story.
Situation: what the process was, such as checking someone's identity.
Task: what pressure you were under to skip it.
Action: what you did and said to keep to the process politely.
Result: what happened, and why the process mattered.
Interviewers listen for: integrity under pressure and good judgement. Many breaches start when someone skips a check to be helpful.
Common mistake: telling a story where you broke the rule and it worked out.

decks.title: Why do you want to move from IT support into security?
decks.answer:
There's no model answer: this has to be your own reason.
Use past, present and future instead of STAR.
Past: what in your IT support work got you interested. Use a real moment.
Present: what you're doing about it now, such as study, labs and certifications.
Future: what you want to do in this role, and why this employer.
Interviewers listen for: genuine interest, proof you're already learning, and that your support experience is a strength.
Common mistake: only saying security pays more or sounds exciting.

decks.title: Ask them: "What does a normal week look like for a junior on this team?"
decks.answer:
Why ask: it shows you're picturing yourself doing the job. It tells you what the job really involves.
A good answer sounds like: a mix of alert triage, tickets, learning time and a named person you'd learn from.
A warning sign: vague answers, or only night shifts and alert queues with no training.

decks.title: Ask them: "How do you support training and certifications?"
decks.answer:
Why ask: it shows you plan to keep growing. It tells you whether they'll invest in you.
A good answer sounds like: paid exams, study time, a training budget or a mentor.
A warning sign: "you'd do that in your own time" with no support at all.

decks.title: Ask them: "Which tools are in your security stack, such as your SIEM and EDR?"
decks.answer:
Why ask: it shows technical interest. It tells you what to study before day one, such as Microsoft Sentinel, Splunk or Defender.
A good answer sounds like: named tools, and how the team uses them.
A warning sign: no central logging at all, which means a lot of manual work.

decks.title: Ask them: "What would success look like in my first 90 days?"
decks.answer:
Why ask: it shows you care about doing well, and it tells you how they'll judge you.
A good answer sounds like: clear goals, such as handling a type of ticket alone or finishing onboarding training.
A warning sign: no idea what success looks like for the role.

owasp-a01.q: An app fetches any URL a user pastes into a “preview link” box. An attacker pastes `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`. What is this?
o: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
Server-side request forgery (SSRF)
Structured Query Language (SQL) injection
owasp-a01.w: SSRF. 169.254.169.254 is the cloud metadata address, and making the server fetch it is SSRF. In 2025 SSRF sits under A01 Broken Access Control. Not SQL injection or XSS: no database query or browser script is involved.

owasp-a02.q: Which is the best long-term fix for misconfiguration across many servers?
o: Asking admins to be more careful
A hardened setup applied automatically
Changing settings by hand after each incident
owasp-a02.w: A hardened setup applied automatically. Manual changes drift. Configuration as code, meaning settings stored as files and applied by tools, keeps every server the same. Not more care or hand fixes: people make mistakes, and settings drift again.

owasp-a03.q: A popular open-source library you use is found to contain a backdoor in its latest release. What do you do first?
o: Update to the newest release
Wait for the vendor to email you
Check your SBOM for that version
owasp-a03.w: Check your SBOM. Scope comes first: the SBOM tells you where the bad version runs, so you can pin or roll back those systems. Waiting wastes time, and updating to the newest release installs the backdoor.

owasp-a04.q: Which of these is a cryptographic failure?
o: Hashing passwords with unsalted MD5
Using parameterised database queries
Requiring two-factor login for admins
owasp-a04.w: Hashing passwords with unsalted MD5. MD5 is fast, and unsalted hashes crack quickly. Passwords need a slow, salted algorithm like Argon2 or bcrypt. Not two-factor login or parameterised queries: both are good security controls.

owasp-a05.q: Text posted in a comment box runs as JavaScript in other users' browsers. What is it, and what's the main fix?
o: XSS; encode output for the HTML context
SQL injection; use parameterised queries
Server-side request forgery; block metadata calls
owasp-a05.w: XSS, fixed by encoding output. XSS is injection into the browser, and encoding stops the browser treating the text as code. Not SQL injection or server-side request forgery: nothing here reaches a database or makes the server fetch a URL.

owasp-a06.q: A gift card checkout lets users retry card numbers without limit. Which category does this mainly fit?
o: A04 Cryptographic Failures
A06 Insecure Design
A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures
owasp-a06.w: A06 Insecure Design. Nobody designed for abuse, so rate limits and per-user caps belong in the design from the start. Not A04: no encryption is involved. A09 might help you notice the guessing, but the missing limit is the root flaw.

owasp-a07.q: Which control best defends against credential stuffing?
o: Longer session timeouts
Hiding the login page address
MFA and breached-password checks
owasp-a07.w: MFA and breached-password checks. Stuffing replays leaked passwords. MFA stops a reused password being enough, and breached-password checks stop reuse. Longer timeouts don't affect logins, and a hidden login page is usually found.

owasp-a08.q: Why didn't code signing protect SolarWinds customers?
o: The signing certificate had expired
Malicious code was signed in the build
Customers had turned signature checks off
owasp-a08.w: Malicious code was signed in the build. A signature proves who built the software, not that the build was clean. So protecting the pipeline matters as much as signing. Not disabled checks or an expired certificate: the checks ran and passed.

owasp-a09.q: What's the most important test for your alerting?
o: Fire a test event and check a person acts
Count how many log lines you store each day
Check that the SIEM licence is still current
owasp-a09.w: Fire a test event and check a person acts. Alerts only matter if someone sees them, so test the whole path from event to human. Log volume and licences don't show whether anyone is told.

owasp-a10.q: What should a user see when your app hits an unexpected error?
o: Nothing, and the action should carry on
The full stack trace, to help them report it
A generic message, with details in your logs
owasp-a10.w: A generic message, with details in your logs. Users get a safe message, developers get the details, and the action stops safely. A full stack trace, a detailed error report, shows attackers how your code is built. Carrying on can leave a transaction half-finished.

inc-change.q: Change Healthcare paid US$22 million. What happened to the stolen data?
o: It was used in further extortion attempts
The attackers proved it was deleted
It was handed back to Change Healthcare
inc-change.w: It was used in further extortion attempts. Paying a ransom doesn't buy certainty, and data from this attack resurfaced later. Not deleted or handed back: attackers' promises can't be checked, and this data came back.

inc-medibank.q: Which two controls would most directly have stopped the Medibank login?
o: MFA on the VPN; admin logins off home PCs
Disk encryption and a bigger firewall
Server antivirus and longer passwords
inc-medibank.w: MFA on the VPN and keeping admin logins off home PCs. The login was stolen from a home PC and worked with no second factor. Not encryption or a firewall: the login itself was valid. Not antivirus or longer passwords: a stolen password works however long it is.

inc-waikato.q: What made recovery at Waikato DHB so slow?
o: Many systems had to be rebuilt and restored
The ransom note was in a foreign language
Staff refused to switch to pen and paper
inc-waikato.w: Many systems had to be rebuilt and restored across a whole health network, which takes weeks. Tested backups and a practised plan shorten that time. Not the ransom note: the ransom wasn't paid. Not staff: they went back to pen and paper.

inc-latitude.q: How did the attackers get a Latitude employee's credentials?
o: Through an attack via a major vendor
By guessing the employee's weak password
By phoning Latitude's IT help desk
inc-latitude.w: Through an attack via a major vendor. The attack came in through the vendor and gave the attackers a Latitude employee's login. The exact vendor route was never fully disclosed. Not guessing or a help desk call: the login came through the vendor.

inc-moveit.q: Many MOVEit victims had never used MOVEit themselves. How were they affected?
o: Their suppliers used it to move their data
Cl0p scanned their office networks
Their staff opened Cl0p phishing emails
inc-moveit.w: Their suppliers used it to move their data. This is third-party risk: your data is only as safe as the tools your suppliers use. Not scanning or phishing: Cl0p exploited MOVEit servers, so these victims were hit through suppliers.

inc-log4shell.q: What did an attacker need to trigger Log4Shell?
o: A crafted string that the app logged
Physical access to the server
An admin password for the server
inc-log4shell.w: A crafted string that the app logged. Usernames, headers and search boxes all got logged, so the attack surface was enormous. Not physical access or an admin password: an attacker only had to get text into a log.

inc-xz.q: Why was the xz backdoor so hard to spot in code review?
o: It hid in test files and build scripts
It was written in assembly language
The project's source code was private
inc-xz.w: It hid in test files and build scripts. The payload was disguised as binary test data, and the script that unpacked it was only in the release tarballs, the packaged downloads. Not assembly: the payload was hidden, not written in an unusual language. Not private code: xz is open source.

inc-crowdstrike.q: Why did many CrowdStrike-affected machines need hands-on fixes?
o: They crashed before remote tools could load
The update had deleted their system files
Staff had forgotten their BitLocker passwords
inc-crowdstrike.w: They crashed before remote tools could load. A machine stuck at a blue screen can't run remote management. Not deleted files: a kernel driver error caused the crash. Not forgotten passwords: BitLocker recovery keys were often needed, but that wasn't the cause.

inc-uber.q: How did the attacker get the contractor to approve an MFA prompt?
o: Spamming prompts, then posing as IT
Exploiting a flaw in the MFA app
Stealing the contractor's phone
inc-uber.w: Spamming prompts, then posing as IT on WhatsApp. This is MFA fatigue plus social engineering, which means tricking people. Number matching or phishing-resistant MFA would have helped. Not an app flaw or a stolen phone: the contractor approved the prompt.

tri-spray.q: Password spraying (T1110.003) sits under which ATT&CK tactic?
o: Exfiltration
Initial Access
Credential Access
tri-spray.w: Credential Access. Brute force and its sub-techniques are ways of getting credentials, so they sit there. Not Initial Access: logging in with the guessed password is a later step. Not Exfiltration: that means stealing data out of a network.

tri-ssh.q: An analyst tags this alert T1110.001. What are they telling the team?
o: It's an internal ticket number
It's an ATT&CK sub-technique: password guessing
It's a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry
tri-ssh.w: It's an ATT&CK sub-technique: password guessing. ATT&CK IDs give every tool and team one name for a behaviour. Not a CVE: those name software flaws. Not a ticket number: T IDs come from the public ATT&CK catalogue.

tri-phish.q: Phishing (T1566) belongs to which ATT&CK tactic?
o: Impact
Exfiltration
Initial Access
tri-phish.w: Initial Access. Phishing is how attackers first get in, so it's an Initial Access technique. Not Exfiltration: that means stealing data out of a network. Not Impact: that means disrupting or destroying systems and data.

tri-macro.q: A user opening a malicious document (T1204.002) maps to which ATT&CK tactic?
o: Execution
Persistence
Exfiltration
tri-macro.w: Execution. User Execution covers tricking someone into running the attacker's code. Not Persistence: that means making malware start again automatically, such as after a reboot. Not Exfiltration: that means stealing data out of a network.

tri-cloudtrail.q: Logging in with stolen valid cloud credentials (T1078.004) is listed under several ATT&CK tactics. Which is one of them?
o: Impact
Exfiltration
Initial Access
tri-cloudtrail.w: Initial Access. Valid Accounts appears under Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation and Stealth (split from Defense Evasion in ATT&CK v19). Not Exfiltration or Impact: signing in gets the attacker in, but doesn't steal or damage data by itself.

inc-capitalone.q: Besides SSRF, what made the Capital One breach so large?
o: The cloud role could reach many buckets
The buckets were open to the public
The firewall was switched off entirely
inc-capitalone.w: The cloud role could reach many buckets. Least privilege on cloud roles limits what stolen credentials can reach. Not public buckets: the attacker needed the stolen credentials. Not a switched-off firewall: the firewall was running but misconfigured.
